entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory organized 1817 from the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory; Alabama achieved statehood December 14, 1819
- **Administrative center:** St. Stephens (territorial capital), then Huntsville, then Cahaba (first state capital)
- **Parent jurisdictions (chronologically):** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–)
- **Prior colonial administrations:** French (Mobile, 1702–1763), British (1763–1780), Spanish (Mobile District, 1780–1813)
- **Population during period:** Sparse at the start of the period; dramatically increased after the Creek War of 1813–1814 opened interior lands to American settlement
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, fur trade; the Mobile area had an established mercantile economy from the colonial period
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (predominant in the interior), Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia arriving in volume after 1814; French Creole and Spanish families in the Mobile coastal region
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist and Methodist circuit riders were the dominant Protestant presence in the interior; Catholic parishes in the Mobile area with roots in the French and Spanish colonial period
- **Key historical events:** Establishment of the Mississippi Territory (1798); expansion of the territory (1804, 1812); Creek War / Battle of Horseshoe Bend (1813–1814); organization of Alabama Territory (1817); Alabama statehood (1819)

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: The Alabama region was not organized as a U.S. territory. The Mobile coastal strip was under Spanish jurisdiction; the interior was governed in practice by Creek and Cherokee nations.
- 1798–1817: The region was part of the Mississippi Territory, with its seat of government far to the west. Records created during this period are Mississippi territorial records.
- 1817–1819: The eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory was organized as the Alabama Territory.
- 1819–present: Alabama was admitted as the 22nd state on December 14, 1819. County organization proceeded rapidly and records began transferring to newly formed county courthouses.
- **Critical rule:** For any event before 1817, search under Mississippi Territory (not Alabama). For events 1817–1819, search Alabama Territory. County-level records begin only as each county was formally organized.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during the territorial period. County-level marriage records began when each county was organized (the earliest FamilySearch collection, Alabama, County Marriages, begins 1809). Statewide birth and death registration did not begin until the 20th century.
- **What exists for ca. 1800:** Marriage bonds and licenses at the county level beginning 1809, once county courts were established. No civil birth or death registration.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1598408, dating 1809–1950)
- **Gaps:** No county-level marriage records predate county formation; no civil birth or death records exist for this period at all
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptism, burial); territorial census enumerations; estate inventories naming heirs

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, with records continuous from the French colonial era); Baptist and Methodist (interior, from the early 1800s)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic sacramental records for Mobile are at the Archdiocese of Mobile archives and have been partially microfilmed by FamilySearch (collection 1986396, Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950, with images). Baptist and Methodist conference records are scattered across local churches and denominational archives.
- **Language:** Catholic records in the Mobile area may be in French or Spanish for the colonial/early American period
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection 1986396 is partially digitized; some records must be requested from the originating church or diocesan archive

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in the present-day Alabama region. According to the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy, Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)), these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery.
- **Federal census:** The 1810 and 1820 federal censuses cover this region. Alabama appears in the 1820 census as a state for the first time.
- **Compiled substitutes:** FamilySearch collection 2016756 (Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890) is name-indexed but has no images. The Mississippi-scope collection 1927171 (Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890) covers territorial-era substitutes with no images.
- **Access:** Federal census images are online at Ancestry and FamilySearch; territorial censuses require contact with ADAH in Montgomery

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins when each county was organized; the FamilySearch collection (1537764, Alabama, Probate Records) dates from 1809
- **Where held:** County probate courts; FamilySearch collection 1537764 has 438,210 indexed records and images
- **Mississippi territorial court records:** FamilySearch collection 1855293 (Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920) covers the territorial period and is indexed with images; relevant for events in present-day Alabama before 1817
- **Browse-only territorial volume:** FamilySearch digitized volume 004512889 (214 images, territorial court and land records, 1808–1819) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a federal land state, not a state-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government, through the General Land Office (now Bureau of Land Management). Original patents are searchable at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, private land claims (for settlers with pre-American titles under French/Spanish/British grants), deeds at the county level, territorial land records
- **Private land claims:** Settlers who held land under Spanish, French, or British grants before American acquisition filed private land claims, adjudicated by federal commissioners. These records are at NARA and are a critical source for the Mobile area and older settlements.
- **Where held:** Federal patents at BLM GLO; territorial land records in FamilySearch volumes 004512889 and 004512890 (browse-only); the Mississippi territorial collection (1919694, Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907) is indexed with images and covers the period directly
- **Access:** BLM GLO is free online; FamilySearch territorial volumes require image-by-image browsing

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812 (including the defense of Mobile); earlier campaigns against Native nations
- **Record types:** Militia service records, pension files, bounty land warrant applications
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pension files, with many digitized on Fold3 and Ancestry); Alabama Department of Archives and History holds some state militia records
- **Creek War specifically:** Pension and bounty land files for Creek War service are at NARA and available via Fold3 (fold3.com)

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has coverage for Alabama, though pre-1820 marked graves are relatively sparse
- **Physical records:** Many early cemeteries were family or church plots with no surviving registers; sexton records, where they exist, are held locally

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (est. 1811) is among the earliest Alabama-area newspapers; Huntsville had early papers from around 1816
- **Where held:** Some early territorial newspapers are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History; Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) has some coverage
- **Content value:** Legal notices (estate, land sales), marriage notices — useful for the period

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (arrival port for coastal settlers and goods); New Orleans was the major regional port
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA; private land claim files document place of origin for colonial settlers
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — search territorial and county court records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family's arrival.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county tax lists
- **Value:** Tax lists are among the few annual records that can substitute for census years; they document a person's presence in a county year by year
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial and early county tax records; some are in the FamilySearch territorial volumes

### Colonial records (pre-1798)
- **French records (1702–1763):** Civil and church records for Mobile and settlements; originals at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm copies at the Mobile Municipal Archives. ([Alabama Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **British records (1763–1780):** Colonial administration records; held at the Public Record Office (The National Archives, Kew, UK)
- **Spanish records (1780–1813):** Mobile District census returns, church registers, and land grants; originals at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain; copies at the Library of Congress. ([Alabama Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (collection 1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census Substitutes, 1810–1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (1986396); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (1927171) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Alabama (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census; Fold3 military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files including Creek War | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including passenger lists, pension files, private land claims | Free to search; some records require ordering |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 2 digitized volumes for Alabama in this period and 1 for the Mississippi Territory — this is a small and likely incomplete picture; additional microfilmed and digitized material exists through the Alabama Department of Archives and History and NARA that does not appear in FamilySearch volume results.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History, Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810), territorial tax lists, county records, military records | In-person; some records available by mail or through their online catalog |
| National Archives (NARA), Southeast Region (Atlanta, GA) | Federal records for Alabama including census, court, land, military | In-person; many records digitized |
| NARA, Washington, DC / College Park | Pension files, private land claim records, territorial records | In-person or order copies; many on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for Mobile District, 1780–1813 | In-person or through the Library of Congress copies |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile, 1702–1763 | In-person; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records; local records | In-person |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records | In-person; some digitized |
| County probate courts (AL) | Deed books, probate files, marriage records from county formation onward | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (the 1810 may be partially accessible; consult ADAH)
- Most territorial tax lists
- Spanish colonial records for Mobile (originals in Seville; copies at Library of Congress — not online in searchable form)
- French colonial records for Mobile (originals in France; microfilm in Mobile)
- British colonial administrative records (The National Archives, Kew)
- Baptist and Methodist church registers from the early interior settlements (scattered among local churches)
- Private land claim adjudication files at NARA (partially available through specialized NARA requests)

## Known record losses
- Record survival for the territorial period is generally thin. The early county courthouses were simple structures and courthouse fires were common across the South through the 19th century. No single catastrophic destruction has been noted for this pre-statehood period, but many early county records simply were never created in a systematic way or have not survived.
- Note that the gap in the record landscape itself is the key hazard: the absence of a record in an online database does not mean the event did not occur — it likely means the record was never digitized, was recorded in a territorial series rather than a state series, or is in a physical repository.

## Research tips
- **The territorial split is the most important gotcha.** Before 1817, search Mississippi Territory records. # Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1780-1820)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Alabama Territory organized 1817 from the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory; Alabama achieved statehood December 14, 1819
- **Administrative center:** St. Stephens (territorial capital), then Huntsville, then Cahaba (first state capital)
- **Parent jurisdictions (chronologically):** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817) → Alabama Territory (1817-1819) → State of Alabama (1819-)
- **Prior colonial administrations:** French (Mobile, 1702-1763), British (1763-1780), Spanish (Mobile District, 1780-1813)
- **Population during period:** Sparse at the opening of the period; dramatically increased after the Creek War of 1813-1814 opened interior lands to American settlement
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, fur trade; the Mobile area had an established mercantile economy from the colonial period
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (predominant in the interior), Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia arriving in volume after 1814; French Creole and Spanish families in the Mobile coastal region
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist and Methodist circuit riders in the interior; Catholic parishes in the Mobile area with roots in the French and Spanish colonial period
- **Key historical events:** Establishment of the Mississippi Territory (1798); expansions (1804, 1812); Creek War / Battle of Horseshoe Bend (1813-1814); organization of Alabama Territory (1817); Alabama statehood (1819)

## Boundary changes

This is a **temporal split with multiple predecessor jurisdictions** — the records do not simply cross a single line:

- **Before 1798:** No organized U.S. territory. The Mobile coastal strip was under Spanish jurisdiction; the interior was Creek and Cherokee country.
- **1798-1817:** The entire region was part of the Mississippi Territory. Records from this period — land, court, tax — are Mississippi territorial records, held at ADAH and NARA.
- **1817-1819:** The eastern portion became the Alabama Territory. Records begin accumulating under this new jurisdiction.
- **1819-present:** State of Alabama. County organization proceeded rapidly; records transferred to county courthouses as counties were formed.

**Critical rule:** For any event before 1817, search under the Mississippi Territory, not Alabama. County-level records begin only as each specific county was formally organized under the Territory, starting with Washington County (1800).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during the territorial period or at statehood in 1819. Statewide birth and death registration did not begin until the early 20th century.
- **What exists for ca. 1800:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses beginning when each county was organized. The FamilySearch collection Alabama, County Marriages (collection 1598408) begins 1809.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; FamilySearch collection 1598408 is indexed with images
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration whatsoever for this period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; estate inventories naming surviving heirs; territorial census enumerations

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, with records continuous from the French colonial era ca. 1702); Baptist and Methodist (interior, from the early 1800s via circuit riders)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic sacramental records for Mobile are at the Archdiocese of Mobile archives and have been partially digitized — FamilySearch collection 1986396 (Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950) has 156,789 indexed records and images. Baptist and Methodist conference records are scattered across local churches and denominational archives.
- **Language:** Catholic records in the Mobile area may be in French or Spanish for the colonial and early American period
- **Digitization level:** Partially indexed + images (FamilySearch 1986396); physical only for most Protestant interior churches

### Census records

- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory conducted enumerations in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that covered the Alabama region. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy, Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)), these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery.
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covers this region under Mississippi Territory. The 1820 census is the first to enumerate Alabama as a state.
- **Compiled substitutes:** FamilySearch collection 2016756 (Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890) is name-indexed with no images. Collection 1927171 (Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890) covers territorial-era substitutes — also indexed with no images.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed (no images) for compiled substitutes; images for federal censuses on Ancestry and FamilySearch; territorial censuses require contact with ADAH

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins when each county was organized; FamilySearch collection 1537764 (Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985) has 438,210 indexed records with images
- **Mississippi territorial court records:** FamilySearch collection 1855293 (Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920) covers events in present-day Alabama before 1817 and is indexed with images
- **Browse-only territorial volume:** FamilySearch volume 004512889 (214 images, territorial court and land records, 1808-1819) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (1537764 and 1855293); browse-only for volume 004512889

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government, through the General Land Office. Original patents are searchable at glorecords.blm.gov. Alabama has no state land office for original grants.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, private land claims (for settlers holding French/Spanish/British grants before American acquisition), deeds at the county level
- **Private land claims:** Settlers with pre-American titles filed private land claims adjudicated by federal commissioners. These files, held at NARA, contain biographical and origin information and are critical for the Mobile area and older settlements.
- **FamilySearch coverage:** Collection 1919694 (Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907) is indexed with images and covers the territorial period directly. Browse-only volumes 004512889 and 004512890 cover territorial land records 1808-1819 and Washington County deed/probate 1803-1820.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (1919694); browse-only (004512889, 004512890); BLM GLO free online for patents

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812 (defense of Mobile); earlier territorial militia actions
- **Record types:** Militia service records, pension files, bounty land warrant applications
- **Where held:** NARA holds service records and pension files; many are digitized on Fold3 (fold3.com, subscription) and Ancestry. ADAH holds some state militia records.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on Fold3/Ancestry for federal pension and service records

### Cemetery records

- **Coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has Alabama coverage, though pre-1820 marked graves are relatively sparse
- **Physical records:** Many early cemeteries were family or church plots with no surviving registers; held locally where they exist at all
- **Digitization level:** Partially indexed (FindAGrave); largely physical only for early period

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (est. 1811) is among the earliest Alabama-area papers; Huntsville had early newspapers from around 1816
- **Where held:** Early territorial newspapers are held at ADAH; Newspapers.com has some coverage
- **Content value:** Legal notices (estate administration, land sales), marriage announcements

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (coastal arrivals); New Orleans was the major regional port
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA; private land claim files document place of origin for colonial-era settlers
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — search territorial and county court records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial and county property and poll tax lists
- **Date range:** Territorial tax lists from the 1800s onward; county tax lists from county formation
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial and early county tax records; some appear in the FamilySearch territorial volumes
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists document year-by-year presence and can substitute for the many census years that simply do not exist for this period

### Colonial records (pre-1798)

This is a distinct research trail for families in the Mobile area or older settlements:

- **French records (1702-1763):** Civil and church records for Mobile; originals at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives
- **British records (1763-1780):** Colonial administrative records; held at The National Archives, Kew, UK
- **Spanish records (1780-1813):** Mobile District census returns, church registers, and land grants; originals at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress

Source: [Alabama Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950 (1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985 (1537764); Alabama, Census Substitutes, 1810-1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950 (1986396); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907 (1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920 (1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census Substitutes, 1792-1890 (1927171) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension files, Creek War records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including passenger lists, pension files, private land claims | Free to search; copies require ordering |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 2 digitized volumes for Alabama in this period (total results: 2) and 1 for the Mississippi Territory — this is a small and likely incomplete picture. Additional microfilmed and digitized material exists through ADAH and NARA that does not appear in FamilySearch volume results.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810), territorial tax lists, early county records, state militia records | In-person; some records via mail or their online catalog |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta, GA | Federal records for Alabama including census, court, land, and military | In-person; many records digitized |
| NARA, Washington DC / College Park, MD | Pension files, private land claim records, territorial records | In-person or copy orders; many on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for Mobile District, 1780-1813 | In-person; Library of Congress holds partial copies |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile, 1702-1763 | In-person; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records; local municipal records | In-person |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records | In-person; some digitized |
| County probate courts (AL) | Deed books, probate files, marriage records from county formation | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online

- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (contact ADAH)
- Most territorial tax lists
- Spanish colonial records for Mobile (originals in Seville; Library of Congress copies not in searchable online form)
- French colonial records for Mobile (originals in Aix-en-Provence; microfilm in Mobile)
- British colonial administrative records (The National Archives, Kew)
- Baptist and Methodist church registers from early interior settlements (scattered among local churches)
- Private land claim adjudication files at NARA (available by specific request; not in general online databases)

## Known record losses

Record survival for the territorial period is generally thin. Early county courthouses were simple structures and courthouse fires were common across the South throughout the 19th century. No single catastrophic record destruction has been documented specifically for this pre-statehood period, but many early county records were never created systematically or have not survived. The most important gap is the near-total absence of civil vital registration — this is not a record loss, it is a record type that was not created at all during this period.

## Research tips

- **The territorial split is the most critical gotcha.** Before 1817, search Mississippi Territory records. The Alabama-labeled FamilySearch collections begin ca. 1809 only because that is when the first Alabama-area counties were organized under the Territory. Governing records before 1809 are in the Mississippi territorial series and territorial volumes. ([Alabama Genealogy, Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Federal land state — search BLM GLO, not a state land office.** Alabama land was distributed by the federal government. Original patents are at glorecords.blm.gov. Alabama has no state land office for original grants.
- **Private land claims are a prime source for Mobile-area families.** If your ancestor held land under a Spanish, French, or British grant, a private land claim file at NARA almost certainly exists and will contain biographical and origin information.
- **Territorial censuses are essential.** The 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 territorial censuses may be the only enumerations of your ancestor before the 1820 federal census. Contact ADAH in Montgomery directly for access.
- **Two FamilySearch territorial volumes are browse-only.** Volume 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808-1819, 214 images) and volume 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate, 1803-1820, 96 images) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. You must examine them image by image with no search capability.
- **No civil vital registration exists for this period.** Church registers — primarily Catholic in Mobile, Baptist/Methodist in the interior — are the only vital record substitutes. Estate inventories and probate files may name heirs and establish family relationships when church records are absent.
- **Tax lists substitute for missing census years.** Annual territorial and county tax lists document year-by-year presence. ADAH holds these for the territorial period.
- **Colonial records require European archives for Mobile-area families.** French and Spanish colonial records naming families are held in Aix-en-Provence and Seville respectively, with partial copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives. ([Alabama Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Check Georgia and Tennessee origin records.** Most Anglo-American settlers who arrived after the Creek War came from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee. Georgia land lottery records (which predate the move) often document the family unit and origin county before migration into Alabama.
- **FamilySearch Alabama wiki place pages did not resolve to Alabama-specific content in this survey.** Consult the Alabama Genealogy page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy for additional jurisdiction-specific guidance.

| National Archives (NARA), Southeast Region (Atlanta, GA) | Federal records for Alabama including census, court, land, military | In-person; many records digitized |
| NARA, Washington, DC / College Park | Pension files, private land claim records, territorial records | In-person or order copies; many on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for Mobile District, 1780–1813 | In-person or through the Library of Congress copies |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile, 1702–1763 | In-person; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records; local records | In-person |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records | In-person; some digitized |
| County probate courts (AL) | Deed books, probate files, marriage records from county formation onward | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (the 1810 may be partially accessible; consult ADAH)
- Most territorial tax lists
- Spanish colonial records for Mobile (originals in Seville; copies at Library of Congress — not online in searchable form)
- French colonial records for Mobile (originals in France; microfilm in Mobile)
- British colonial administrative records (The National Archives, Kew)
- Baptist and Methodist church registers from the early interior settlements (scattered among local churches)
- Private land claim adjudication files at NARA (partially available through specialized NARA requests)

## Known record losses
- Record survival for the territorial period is generally thin. The early county courthouses were simple structures and courthouse fires were common across the South through the 19th century. No single catastrophic destruction has been noted for this pre-statehood period, but many early county records simply were never created in a systematic way or have not survived.
- Note that the gap in the record landscape itself is the key hazard: the absence of a record in an online database does not mean the event did not occur — it likely means the record was never digitized, was recorded in a territorial series rather than a state series, or is in a physical repository.

## Research tips
- **The territorial split is the most important gotcha.** Before 1817, search Mississippi Territory records. The Alabama-labeled FamilySearch collections mostly begin 1809 at the earliest because that is when the first Alabama-area counties were organized under the Territory — but the governing records before then are in the Mississippi territorial series.
- **Federal land state:** Alabama land was distributed by the federal government. The BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) is the starting point for original patents. Do not search a state land office — Alabama has none for original grants.
- **Private land claims:** If your ancestor lived in the Mobile area or was a pre-American settler, a private land claim file at NARA is likely to exist and will contain biographical and origin information.
- **Territorial censuses are critical.** The 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 territorial censuses may be the only enumeration capturing your ancestor before the 1820 federal census. Contact ADAH in Montgomery directly.
- **Colonial records require European archives** for the Mobile area. French and Spanish colonial records naming families are held in Aix-en-Provence and Seville, with partial copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives. ([Alabama Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Two FamilySearch territorial volumes (004512889 and 004512890) are browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. They cover territorial court/land records 1808–1819 and Washington County deed/probate 1803–1820. You must browse them image by image.
- **Church records substitute for absent civil registration.** No civil birth or death registration existed in this period. Baptism and burial registers — primarily Catholic in Mobile, Baptist and Methodist in the interior — are the only vital record alternatives.
- **Tax lists as census substitutes.** Annual territorial and early county tax lists document presence year by year between the sparse census years. ADAH holds these.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** The Tennessee Valley (northern Alabama) was also settled from Tennessee and Virginia; Georgia records (particularly land lottery records) document many families who subsequently moved into Alabama. Check Georgia archives for origin records of families arriving from that direction.

**Arkansas Region Before 1800 — Locality Guide Summary**

The Arkansas area before 1800 was not yet a U.S. state or organized territory. It was a small Spanish (and earlier, French) colonial district centered on **Arkansas Post**, one of the oldest European settlements in the lower Mississippi Valley. Records are fragmentary, held across multiple repositories, and mostly unavailable as indexed online searches.

| Record Type | Where Held |

| **Notarial & ecclesiastical records** | New Orleans repositories (Orleans Parish notarial archives, Archdiocese of New Orleans) |

### Critical Context

- **No FamilySearch indexed collections** exist for this period in Arkansas.
- **No U.S. federal census** covers Arkansas before 1820.
- The district was **administered from New Orleans** — so residents appear in Louisiana-based notarial, court, and church records just as often as in anything generated at Arkansas Post itself. Colonial Arkansas records are essentially inseparable from Louisiana records.

Build a research plan anchored on the ancestor's likely ethnicity, religion, and approximate date of residence in the district — those factors determine which specific repositories to contact first.

After the Louisiana Purchase, American law required holders of Spanish grants to file confirmation claims with the Board of Land Commissioners (from 1805); these English-language claims are more accessible than the original Spanish documents and name grantees with their land-holding history.

French Creole naming conventions persisted under Spanish rule — expect dit names, compound given names, and the same individual appearing under both French and Spanish name forms in different record series.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formal name during period:** District of Arkansas (Distrito de Arkansas), subordinate to the Province of Louisiana under Spanish colonial administration
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas / Puesto de Arkansas)
- **Parent jurisdiction (civil):** Province of Louisiana, governed from New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction (ecclesiastical):** Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas, New Orleans
- **Period of Spanish control:** 1763-1800
- **Earlier French period:** 1686-1763
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur trade, military garrison, river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish officials/soldiers, Quapaw Nation, enslaved Africans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively

## Boundary changes
The Arkansas region before 1800 was not a county — it was a district-level military and civil post within the Province of Louisiana. All civil authority flowed: Arkansas Post commandant → Governor in New Orleans → Captaincy General in Havana → Spain. Records may survive at any of these administrative levels. After 1803 (Louisiana Purchase) American territorial government introduced county-level organization; Arkansas County was organized in 1813.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration during the Spanish colonial period. All vital event recording was the exclusive function of the Roman Catholic Church.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 008814402 — 64 images, Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800. **Browse-only. Spanish/Latin. 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.**
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (originals/transcriptions); Arkansas History Commission (transcriptions); FamilySearch (digitized volume above).

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic only.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons and Native Americans), marriages, burials. Bishop visitation records may be at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.
- **Language:** Spanish, Latin; French in pre-1763 registers.
- **Digitization level: Browse-only images** (volume 008814402).

### Census records (padrones)
- **Type:** Spanish colonial padrones — household enumerations naming heads of household, family members, servants, and enslaved persons.
- **Known surviving examples:** 1790s padrones for the Arkansas district.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission (transcripts); Archivo General de Indias, Seville (originals, Papeles de Cuba section); Library of Congress (microfilm of selected AGI materials).
- **No FamilySearch indexed collection covers pre-1800 Arkansas padrones.**
- **Digitization level: Physical only / microfilm.**

### Land records
- **System:** Spanish colonial land concessions (concesiones de tierra). After 1803, holders filed American confirmation claims.
- **Types:** Concession petitions, grants, confirmations, plats; American State Papers Public Lands (vols. 2-4) documents confirmations.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; NARA (American confirmation records); Archivo General de Indias (original Spanish grants); BLM GLO (American patents post-1803 only).
- **Digitization level: Mostly physical or microfilm.** American State Papers freely online at HathiTrust/LOC.

### Military records
- **Context:** Arkansas Post was a Spanish military garrison. Muster rolls, service records (hojas de servicio), and officer correspondence exist.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Archivo General Militar de Segovia, Spain; Arkansas History Commission (some transcripts).
- **Digitization level: Physical only** (in Spain; some digitized on PARES).

### Probate and court records
- **System:** The commandant acted as local magistrate. Complex matters went to New Orleans.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission (some transcripts); Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans.
- **Digitization level: Physical only.**

### Notarial records
- **Context:** Notarial acts (sales, contracts, manumissions, marriage contracts) are a primary source in the French/Spanish legal tradition.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives; Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Digitization level: Physical only** for colonial series.

### Tax records
- No separate property tax series. Padrones sometimes recorded property/livestock. Serve same substitute function as American tax lists.

### Cemetery records
- Burial records are within the sacramental registers. Arkansas Post National Memorial (NPS) may hold some local history records.

### Newspapers
- No newspaper operated in the Arkansas district before 1800. Not a source for this period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) 1763-1800, 64 images, browse-only, Spanish/Latin | Free |
| Archivo General de Indias (PARES) | pares.mcu.es — Papeles de Cuba section; many documents digitized | Free |
| HathiTrust / Library of Congress | American State Papers, Public Lands (vols. 2-4) — Spanish grant confirmations | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (totalResults: 1, no nextPageToken) — that is the complete FamilySearch digitized set for pre-1810 Arkansas. collections_search returned 3 indexed collections for Arkansas, none covering pre-1800.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Colonial padrones, sacramental register transcriptions, land concession papers, Arkansas Post judicial records | In-person; arkansasheritage.com |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives | Sacramental registers from Arkansas Post Catholic mission | Contact archives directly |
| Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans, LA | Colonial Louisiana court records, notarial acts, entry records | In-person; partial online catalog |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives | Notarial acts including Arkansas Post residents' transactions | In-person; some online indexes |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Diocese of Louisiana and Floridas records, bishop visitations | Contact archives directly |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Microfilm of selected Archivo General de Indias materials for Spanish Louisiana | In-person or interlibrary loan |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Master repository for all Spanish colonial records: administrative, military, land, ecclesiastical | pares.mcu.es (many digitized); in-person or image requests |
| Archivo General Militar de Segovia, Spain | Officer service records (hojas de servicio) for Arkansas Post military personnel | Correspondence or in-person |
| Arkansas Post National Memorial (NPS) | Site records, local history | Contact the memorial directly |
| NARA, Washington D.C. / Fort Worth, TX | American territorial land commission records post-1803 | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Padrones (colonial censuses) — Arkansas History Commission and Library of Congress microfilm
- Spanish land concession originals — Archivo General de Indias and Arkansas History Commission
- Colonial military records — Archivo General de Indias and Archivo General Militar de Segovia
- Notarial acts (colonial series) — New Orleans Notarial Archives and Louisiana Historical Center
- Arkansas Post judicial/court records — Arkansas History Commission only
- Diocesan correspondence and bishop visitation records — Archdiocese of New Orleans
- Pre-1763 French-period sacramental registers — Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission

## Known record losses
- Arkansas Post was physically relocated several times and suffered flooding and military action; gaps in sacramental registers are expected.
- New Orleans colonial records suffered damage from fire, humidity, and Civil War disruptions.
- The Archivo General de Indias in Seville is the most complete surviving repository — materials forwarded to Spain are better preserved than what was retained locally at the post.

## Research tips
- **PARES (pares.mcu.es) is your primary online resource.** Search the Papeles de Cuba section of the Archivo General de Indias for Louisiana/Arkansas district records. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- Search Louisiana repositories alongside Arkansas repositories — residents regularly transacted business in New Orleans.
- The FamilySearch digitized volume (008814402) must be browsed in Spanish; use the Diocese of Little Rock transcription as a faster starting point.
- Spanish land grant confirmation claims in American State Papers, Public Lands (vols. 2-4) are freely available online and name colonial-era grantees.
- Padrones name entire households including children and enslaved persons — the Arkansas History Commission transcripts are the starting point.
- Do not rely on any federal census before 1820; the first U.S. federal census for present-day Arkansas is 1820.
- French Creole naming conventions persisted under Spanish rule — expect dit names and both French and Spanish name forms for the same person.
- After the Louisiana Purchase, search American territorial land commission records (from 1805) for English-language confirmation claims citing Spanish grants.

This guide covers the Arkansas region before 1800 — a place that did not yet exist as a U.S. state or even as an organized American territory. The area was a small Spanish (and earlier, French) colonial district centered on Arkansas Post, one of the oldest European settlements in the lower Mississippi Valley. The records that survive are fragmentary, held across multiple continents, and mostly not searchable by name online: one browse-only, Spanish-language volume of church registers on FamilySearch; transcripts of colonial household censuses (padrones) and court records at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock; original Spanish administrative, military, and land records at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville (many now freely digitized at pares.mcu.es); and notarial and ecclesiastical records in New Orleans repositories. There are no FamilySearch indexed collections for this period, and no federal census exists for Arkansas before 1820. The most important warning for this research is that colonial-era Arkansas records are inseparable from Louisiana records — the district was administered from New Orleans, and residents appear in Louisiana-based notarial, court, and church records just as often as in anything generated at the post itself.

The next step is to use this survey as the foundation for a research plan: identifying which specific repositories to contact first based on what is known about your ancestor's likely ethnicity, religion, and approximate date of residence in the district.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formal name during period:** District of Arkansas (Distrito de Arkansas), subordinate to the Province of Louisiana under Spanish colonial administration
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas / Puesto de Arkansas)
- **Parent jurisdiction (civil):** Province of Louisiana, governed from New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction (ecclesiastical):** Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas, New Orleans
- **Period of Spanish control:** 1763-1800
- **Earlier French period:** 1686-1763
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur trade, military garrison, river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish officials/soldiers, Quapaw Nation, enslaved Africans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively

## Boundary changes
The Arkansas region before 1800 was not a county — it was a district-level military and civil post within the Province of Louisiana. All civil authority flowed: Arkansas Post commandant → Governor in New Orleans → Captaincy General in Havana → Spain. Records may survive at any of these administrative levels. After 1803 (Louisiana Purchase) American territorial government introduced county-level organization; Arkansas County was organized in 1813.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration during the Spanish colonial period. All vital event recording was the exclusive function of the Roman Catholic Church.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 008814402 — 64 images, Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800. **Browse-only. Spanish/Latin. 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.**
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (originals/transcriptions); Arkansas History Commission (transcriptions); FamilySearch (digitized volume above).

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic only.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons and Native Americans), marriages, burials. Bishop visitation records may be at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.
- **Language:** Spanish, Latin; French in pre-1763 registers.
- **Digitization level: Browse-only images** (volume 008814402).

### Census records (padrones)
- **Type:** Spanish colonial padrones — household enumerations naming heads of household, family members, servants, and enslaved persons.
- **Known surviving examples:** 1790s padrones for the Arkansas district.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission (transcripts); Archivo General de Indias, Seville (originals, Papeles de Cuba section); Library of Congress (microfilm of selected AGI materials).
- **No FamilySearch indexed collection covers pre-1800 Arkansas padrones.**
- **Digitization level: Physical only / microfilm.**

### Land records
- **System:** Spanish colonial land concessions (concesiones de tierra). After 1803, holders filed American confirmation claims.
- **Types:** Concession petitions, grants, confirmations, plats; American State Papers Public Lands (vols. 2-4) documents confirmations.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; NARA (American confirmation records); Archivo General de Indias (original Spanish grants); BLM GLO (American patents post-1803 only).
- **Digitization level: Mostly physical or microfilm.** American State Papers freely online at HathiTrust/LOC.

### Military records
- **Context:** Arkansas Post was a Spanish military garrison. Muster rolls, service records (hojas de servicio), and officer correspondence exist.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Archivo General Militar de Segovia, Spain; Arkansas History Commission (some transcripts).
- **Digitization level: Physical only** (in Spain; some digitized on PARES).

### Probate and court records
- **System:** The commandant acted as local magistrate. Complex matters went to New Orleans.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission (some transcripts); Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans.
- **Digitization level: Physical only.**

### Notarial records
- **Context:** Notarial acts (sales, contracts, manumissions, marriage contracts) are a primary source in the French/Spanish legal tradition.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives; Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Digitization level: Physical only** for colonial series.

### Tax records
- No separate property tax series. Padrones sometimes recorded property/livestock. Serve same substitute function as American tax lists.

### Cemetery records
- Burial records are within the sacramental registers. Arkansas Post National Memorial (NPS) may hold some local history records.

### Newspapers
- No newspaper operated in the Arkansas district before 1800. Not a source for this period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) 1763-1800, 64 images, browse-only, Spanish/Latin | Free |
| Archivo General de Indias (PARES) | pares.mcu.es — Papeles de Cuba section; many documents digitized | Free |
| HathiTrust / Library of Congress | American State Papers, Public Lands (vols. 2-4) — Spanish grant confirmations | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (totalResults: 1, no nextPageToken) — that is the complete FamilySearch digitized set for pre-1810 Arkansas. collections_search returned 3 indexed collections for Arkansas, none covering pre-1800.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Colonial padrones, sacramental register transcriptions, land concession papers, Arkansas Post judicial records | In-person; arkansasheritage.com |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives | Sacramental registers from Arkansas Post Catholic mission | Contact archives directly |
| Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans, LA | Colonial Louisiana court records, notarial acts, entry records | In-person; partial online catalog |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives | Notarial acts including Arkansas Post residents' transactions | In-person; some online indexes |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Diocese of Louisiana and Floridas records, bishop visitations | Contact archives directly |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Microfilm of selected Archivo General de Indias materials for Spanish Louisiana | In-person or interlibrary loan |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Master repository for all Spanish colonial records: administrative, military, land, ecclesiastical | pares.mcu.es (many digitized); in-person or image requests |
| Archivo General Militar de Segovia, Spain | Officer service records (hojas de servicio) for Arkansas Post military personnel | Correspondence or in-person |
| Arkansas Post National Memorial (NPS) | Site records, local history | Contact the memorial directly |
| NARA, Washington D.C. / Fort Worth, TX | American territorial land commission records post-1803 | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Padrones (colonial censuses) — Arkansas History Commission and Library of Congress microfilm
- Spanish land concession originals — Archivo General de Indias and Arkansas History Commission
- Colonial military records — Archivo General de Indias and Archivo General Militar de Segovia
- Notarial acts (colonial series) — New Orleans Notarial Archives and Louisiana Historical Center
- Arkansas Post judicial/court records — Arkansas History Commission only
- Diocesan correspondence and bishop visitation records — Archdiocese of New Orleans
- Pre-1763 French-period sacramental registers — Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission

## Known record losses
- Arkansas Post was physically relocated several times and suffered flooding and military action; gaps in sacramental registers are expected.
- New Orleans colonial records suffered damage from fire, humidity, and Civil War disruptions.
- The Archivo General de Indias in Seville is the most complete surviving repository — materials forwarded to Spain are better preserved than what was retained locally at the post.

## Research tips
- **PARES (pares.mcu.es) is your primary online resource.** Search the Papeles de Cuba section of the Archivo General de Indias for Louisiana/Arkansas district records. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- Search Louisiana repositories alongside Arkansas repositories — residents regularly transacted business in New Orleans.
- The FamilySearch digitized volume (008814402) must be browsed in Spanish; use the Diocese of Little Rock transcription as a faster starting point.
- Spanish land grant confirmation claims in American State Papers, Public Lands (vols. 2-4) are freely available online and name colonial-era grantees.
- Padrones name entire households including children and enslaved persons — the Arkansas History Commission transcripts are the starting point.
- Do not rely on any federal census before 1820; the first U.S. federal census for present-day Arkansas is 1820.
- French Creole naming conventions persisted under Spanish rule — expect dit names and both French and Spanish name forms for the same person.
- After the Louisiana Purchase, search American territorial land commission records (from 1805) for English-language confirmation claims citing Spanish grants.

Here is the locality guide's full response:

---

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Pre-Statehood / Northwest Territory, 1787–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Ohio did not exist as a jurisdiction in 1790. The entire present-day state was part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio achieved statehood on March 1, 1803. The territorial seat was Marietta (1788); Chillicothe became the later capital.

---

## Boundary Changes

Only **two counties** existed within present-day Ohio as of 1790:

- **Washington County** (organized July 1788): Covered most of southeastern Ohio, including the Ohio Company's settlement at Marietta.
- **Hamilton County** (organized January 1790): Covered the Cincinnati area, carved from Washington County.

If an ancestor lived in territory not yet organized into a county, there was **no civil jurisdiction below the territorial level** — no courthouse, no county clerk, no county court.

Additionally, Ohio is divided into **three distinct land-grant systems** that are geographic, not temporal — and each has its own separate repository:

| District | Location | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| Virginia Military District | Between Scioto & Little Miami rivers | Virginia State Library, Richmond, VA |
| Connecticut Western Reserve | Northeastern Ohio | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| U.S. Public Land Survey | Most of the remainder | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) |

Identifying the district before searching land records is essential — they have completely different archives.

---

## Available Record Types Despite Documentation Gaps

### 🏆 Land Records — Best Starting Point
- FamilySearch: **Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840** (235K records, images online): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187
- One territorial browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 005112233): 51 images, 1788–1799, **0% name-indexed**.
- Federal patents: BLM GLO at glorecords.blm.gov (free).
- Virginia Military District warrants: Virginia State Library (not digitized).

### 💍 Marriage Records
- Civil vital registration did not exist in 1790 (no births, no deaths recorded).
- **Marriage records only**, starting at county formation.
- FamilySearch: **Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013** (1.5M records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785

### ⛪ Church Records
- Primary substitute for births (baptisms) and deaths (burials).
- Very sparse — organized congregations barely existed in 1790.
- FamilySearch: **Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950** (678K records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917

### 🎖 Military Records — Highly Recommended
- Many 1790 Ohio settlers were Revolutionary War veterans who came for bounty land.
- **Pension files at NARA** are biographical gold — first-person declarations naming family, wife, children, and post-war Ohio residence.
- Access via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry.
- Also relevant: Northwest Indian War records (1790–1795).

### 📋 Tax Records
- The earliest practical substitute for census gaps.
- FamilySearch: **Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850** (346K records): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542
- One Washington County tax volume (imageGroupNumber 005112240): 73 images, 1799–1803, 12% indexed.

### 📜 Census Records
- **The 1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory.** There is no practical 1790 Ohio census.
- The **1800 federal census** is the first useful enumeration — indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### 📰 Newspapers
- No Ohio newspaper existed in 1790. The first (Cincinnati) began in November 1793.
- Limited value until ~1800. Chronicling America (loc.gov/chroniclingamerica) and Newspapers.com are access points.

### ⚰️ Cemetery Records
- Formal cemeteries barely existed. Most 1790 burials were on family land or informal church plots.
- Find A Grave covers some pioneer burials, but coverage is sparse.
- No sexton records for 1790 exist.

---

## Known Gaps and Record Losses
Gaps are **structural, not catastrophic** — the county infrastructure was so new that few records were generated in the first place. No major courthouse fire is documented for this period. No Ohio territorial census for 1790 is known to survive.

---

## Key Research Tips
