Here is the locality guide for early 1800s New Orleans, as returned by the subagent:

---

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Record Losses — The Critical Starting Point

New Orleans suffered exceptional record losses that every researcher must understand:

**Pre-period fires:**
- **1788 Great Fire** — Destroyed 856 buildings and took many French colonial records with them.
- **1794 Good Friday Fire** — A second catastrophe eliminated more colonial-era documentation.

These fires predate the 1800–1850 window but their effects are felt throughout it. People in their 40s–60s in 1820 were born before those fires — their baptismal records and parents' marriage records may simply not exist locally.

**Ongoing hazards:**
- Yellow fever epidemics caused institutional continuity gaps; burial/death registers can be chaotic during peak epidemic years.
- Periodic flooding and hurricanes caused physical record deterioration throughout the 19th century.

---

## Substitute Strategies When Records Are Lost

| What was lost | Where to look instead |
|---|---|
| Pre-1788 French colonial records | Spanish colonial records (1763–); surviving notarial acts and church registers in Spain's **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville |
| Pre-1794 records | French colonial records at the **Archives nationales d'outre-mer**, Aix-en-Provence, France |
| Flood/hurricane-damaged originals | Microfilm copies made before the damage, held at FamilySearch or NARA |
| Pre-1837 civil marriage records | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; notarial marriage contracts |
| Pre-1819 civil death records | Church burial registers; newspaper death notices |

---

## Records That Survived and Where to Find Them

### Church Records *(most important vital record substitute)*
- **St. Louis Cathedral** maintains sacramental registers from 1731 (with gaps). This covers Catholic baptisms, marriages, and burials for people of all racial/legal statuses, including free people of color and enslaved individuals.
- **FamilySearch:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) — indexed, with images.
- **Also held at:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (records not yet digitized).

### Notarial Records *(irreplaceable for early New Orleans)*
Louisiana's notarial system required property sales, contracts, manumissions, marriage contracts, and successions to be executed before a licensed notary. A single notarial act can substitute for a birth record, marriage certificate, deed, will, and manumission all at once.

- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds **30+ million pages** of notarial acts from 1734. This is the single most important physical repository — and most of it is **not online**.
- **FamilySearch** has only one digitized volume: image group 004990115, covering 1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only (no name index), in French and English. This is the extent of what is online.
- **Access:** In-person in New Orleans; contact the center for research appointments.

### Civil Vital Records
- **Deaths (indexed):** "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (FamilySearch collection 1543892) — index only, no images.
- **Marriages:** "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (collection 1798054) — indexed, with images.
- **Births:** Civil registration is sparse before statehood infrastructure was in place; church records fill the gap.

### Probate / Succession Records
Louisiana uses the term *succession* (not probate) and *tutorship* (not guardianship) — civil law concepts from the Napoleonic Code. Succession inventories can name heirs, describe property, and name enslaved people with age and sometimes origin.
- **FamilySearch:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) — indexed, with images.
- **Also held at:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives.

### Census Records
Federal censuses from 1810, 1820, 1830, and 1840 cover New Orleans. 1840 is name-indexed for heads of household only. Free people of color appear in the main population schedule throughout.

### Land Records
Louisiana uses the French long-lot system (arpents), not the US township-and-range system. Post-1803 confirmed colonial land grants are searchable at the **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov). Pre-1803 grants are at the Louisiana State Archives and New Orleans Notarial Archives.

### Newspaper Records
New Orleans papers (Louisiana Gazette from 1804, Daily Picayune from 1837, and others) carried death notices, marriage announcements, succession notices, and — critically — **runaway enslaved person advertisements** with detailed physical descriptions, names, origins, and skills.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (subscription); physical/microfilm at the Historic New Orleans Collection, Tulane University, and the New Orleans Public Library.

### Records for Enslaved and Free People of Color
New Orleans had an unusually large and legally distinct free Black community under Louisiana civil law. Key sources:
- Notarial acts of sale, manumissions, and contracts naming enslaved people → New Orleans Notarial Archives
- Succession inventories naming enslaved people → probate records above
- Free persons of color registration papers → Louisiana State Archives
- Free persons of color notarial acts, deeds, successions → Orleans Parish court records and Notarial Archives
- Runaway slave advertisements → newspapers

---

## Key Physical Repositories

| Repository | What they hold |
|---|---|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | 30M+ pages of notarial acts from 1734 — the essential repository |
| **Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge** | Territorial/state records; tax rolls; land records; free persons of color registrations |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Church registers not yet digitized; cemetery sexton records |
| **Historic New Orleans Collection** | Manuscripts, maps, newspapers; strong antebellum coverage |
| **Tulane University Howard-Tilton Memorial Library** | Local histories, newspaper microfilm |
| **Louisiana Division, New Orleans Public Library** | Free people of color manuscripts; city directories; newspaper microfilm |
| **NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta)** | Federal records for Louisiana post-1803 |

---

## Key Practical Tips

1. **The notarial records are not optional.** For early New Orleans, they are the backbone of research. Most exist only in person at the Notarial Archives Research Center.
2. **Records are in French and Spanish, not just English.** Colonial-era through roughly the 1820s are predominantly French. Researchers will need translation help for the originals.
3. **Three governing regimes = three record systems.** French (1718–1763), Spanish (1763–1803), and American (1803+) each created records in different languages and formats.
4. **City directories as census substitutes.** New Orleans had directories from the 1820s onward — useful for placing individuals at specific addresses between censuses. Available at the Historic New Orleans Collection and New Orleans Public Library.
5. **Look in Spain and France for colonial-era ancestors.** If an ancestor's early-life records were destroyed in 1788 or 1794, the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the Archives nationales d'outre-mer (Aix-en-Provence) may be the only recourse.
6. **Check adjoining parishes.** Families near city borders may have records in Jefferson Parish (west), St. Bernard Parish (southeast), or St. Tammany Parish (north).

---

The single most important takeaway: the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds tens of millions of pages that are not online. For most pre-1837 vital events and all major property/legal transactions, an in-person or correspondence visit there is likely unavoidable for serious early New Orleans research.

---

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718, passed to Spanish colonial administration in 1763, reverted briefly to France in 1800-1803, and became part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase in April 1803. Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans itself, seat of Orleans Parish (Louisiana uses parishes, not counties, as its primary civil division — a direct inheritance of French and Spanish colonial administration)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Territory (1804-1812), then State of Louisiana (1812-present)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tool for this place and period. According to Wikipedia, New Orleans was one of the largest US cities by 1840. Census records are the primary source for specific figures.
- **Economy:** Port trade (cotton, sugar, enslaved persons), maritime commerce, and an active mercantile class. The Mississippi River made New Orleans the dominant commercial entrepot of the Gulf South.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, Anglo-Americans arriving after the Louisiana Purchase, free people of color (a uniquely large and legally distinct class in Louisiana civil law), enslaved African Americans, recent immigrants from Germany, Ireland, and Saint-Domingue (Haiti).
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (the dominant colonial institution), with growing Protestant congregations (Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal) after 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803), Battle of New Orleans (1815), repeated yellow fever epidemics (1800s-1850s), ongoing floods and hurricanes. Critically for record survival: catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records before this period even begins.

---

## Boundary changes

- Before 1803: Records were created under French (1718-1763), then Spanish (1763-1800), then briefly French (1800-1803) colonial administration. Spanish-era records use Spanish-language forms and administrative categories.
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase. The U.S. territorial government began generating its own record series. Existing Spanish and French series continued in transition until American administrative forms took over.
- 1804-1812: Orleans Territory. Federal territorial records apply.
- 1812: Louisiana statehood. State-level civil infrastructure begins.
- **Important quirk:** The boundaries of Orleans Parish as a civil division were stable throughout the early 1800s, but the governing legal framework changed three times (French/Spanish/American) within living memory of people in this period. Record formats, languages, and creating institutions each shifted accordingly.

---

## Known record losses — this section is critical for this locality

This is where the guide must be most direct. New Orleans suffered exceptional record losses:

**1788 Great Fire:** Destroyed 856 buildings in the colonial city center. Many French colonial administrative records, including early church registers and governmental papers, were lost. This predates our 1800-1850 window, but it eliminated many records people in that window might have cited as precedents.

**1794 Good Friday Fire:** A second devastating fire destroyed another large section of the city. Again, pre-1800 records are the main casualties, but surviving copies or extracts made before 1800 may be the only access point for colonial-era facts that surface in early 1800s documents.

**Yellow fever epidemics:** Mass deaths in 1800s-1850s generated extraordinary mortality volumes but also killed record-keepers, disrupted institutions, and caused gaps in continuity of registration.

**Flooding and hurricane damage:** Periodic flooding damaged physical records held in low-lying repositories throughout the 19th century.

**What this means for the researcher:** Do not assume a record was never created simply because it is not found online or in one repository. The research strategy for early New Orleans specifically requires checking for copies, transcripts, microfilmed surrogates, and parallel records created by different institutions (church vs. civil vs. notarial) that covered the same events.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Level and start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records resolved to a generic page rather than a Louisiana-specific article, so I cannot give a registration start date sourced from that page without fabricating it. What the tools did return: the "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" collection (FamilySearch collection 1543892) begins in 1819, and "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957" (collection 1798054) begins in 1837 — these dates bracket when indexed civil registration records become findable, but the FamilySearch Wiki did not confirm what the law required or at what administrative level in those years.
- **What exists:** Civil registration for births, marriages, and deaths. The statewide death index (collection 1543892, 2,345,678 records, index only — 0 images) covers 1819-1964. Parish marriages (collection 1798054, 567,890 records, with images) cover 1837-1957.
- **Gaps:** Before statewide infrastructure was in place (roughly before 1819 for deaths, before 1837 for marriage registration), civil registration was sparse or nonexistent at the state level. Church records are the primary vital record source for 1800-1819 and remain a parallel source throughout the period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (see Church records below); notarial acts (marriages solemnized before a notary); newspaper notices.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant); Protestant congregations (Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal) established post-1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. St. Louis Cathedral in the French Quarter has maintained sacramental registers from 1731 (with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires). These are among the most important surviving sources for early New Orleans families of all ethnicities and legal statuses, including free people of color and records of enslaved individuals.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905) covers 1718-1925 and contains 987,654 records with 493,827 images. This is indexed, so it is name-searchable. However, the record count should be treated as an indicator, not a verified total — the tool returned it and I am reporting it as returned.
- **Language:** Colonial-era and early American-era records are predominantly in French. Spanish-era records are in Spanish. After 1803, English appears increasingly. Researchers must be able to read French (and sometimes Latin for sacramental records) to use the originals.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; FamilySearch microfilm and the collection above; the Historic New Orleans Collection.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** New Orleans appears in federal censuses from 1810 onward (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 fall within the period). The 1800 census for Orleans Territory exists but coverage is partial. The 1890 census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire — this does not affect our period, but researchers should know the pattern of census losses nationally.
- **Territorial/state census:** Louisiana conducted some non-federal enumerations; the Louisiana Census wiki page returned a generic article rather than state-specific data, so I cannot confirm specific off-year census dates from that source.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for this period are indexed on Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). The 1840 federal census is name-indexed for heads of household only — other family members are tallied by age and sex brackets.
- **Slave schedules:** Federal slave schedules (1850 onward) list enslaved people by age and sex only, without names, under the enslaver's name. Pre-1850 censuses list enslaved people in aggregate under enslaver households. Free people of color appear in the main population schedule throughout.

### Probate and court records (successions and tutorships)

- **Louisiana civil law distinction:** Louisiana uses the term "succession" rather than probate, and "tutorship" rather than guardianship. These are civil law concepts derived from the Napoleonic Code, not common law. The succession record is the primary probate equivalent.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341) covers 1756-1984 with 456,789 records and 228,394 images. This collection reaches well into our period.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives; FamilySearch (partially).
- **Value:** Succession inventories can name heirs, describe property (including enslaved people by name, age, and sometimes origin), and document family relationships in detail absent from vital records.

### Notarial records

- **This is the most distinctive record class for New Orleans.** Louisiana's notarial system, inherited from French and Spanish colonial practice, required that a wide range of legal acts — property sales, contracts, manumissions of enslaved people, business agreements, marriage contracts, successions — be executed before a licensed notary. These acts were recorded in notarial registers that are separate from the courts.
- **Volume search result:** FamilySearch has one digitized volume for Orleans Parish in this period: image group 004990115, covering 1803-1820, 167 images, in French and English, recording "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)." This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image. The parenthetical "surviving microfilm copies" in the record type is significant: it confirms that what FamilySearch holds are microfilm copies of surviving originals, not the complete notarial series.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center:** According to the wiki_search result (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters), this center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734. This is the primary repository. Access is in-person or by correspondence in New Orleans. Much of this material is not online.
- **Digitization level:** The single FamilySearch volume is browse-only images. The vast majority of notarial acts exist only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives — physical access required.
- **Language:** Early acts are in French or Spanish; post-1803 acts increasingly in English, but French continued well into the 1840s.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** New Orleans and surrounding Louisiana use the French long-lot system (arpents), not the US rectangular township-and-range system. Lot descriptions in deeds reference arpent measurements and front-on-the-river orientation. Researchers unfamiliar with this system should orient themselves before reading land descriptions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pre-1803 Spanish and French crown grants; after 1803, the US General Land Office confirmed (or disputed) colonial-era grants through the Board of Land Commissioners. Federal land patents for confirmed grants are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov).
- **Types:** Colonial grants (French and Spanish), American patents, property deeds, mortgage acts (frequently executed before notaries, not courthouses), tax assessments.
- **Where held:** Colonial grants — Louisiana State Archives and the New Orleans Notarial Archives; post-1803 confirmed patents — BLM GLO; property deeds — Orleans Parish Conveyance Office (which holds the equivalent of a deed registry); tax records — Louisiana State Archives.
- **The Louisiana Land and Property wiki page** returned generic content rather than a Louisiana-specific article, so I cannot cite article-specific details beyond what the tools returned.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812, Battle of New Orleans (January 1815), various territorial militia musters.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (National Archives, Washington DC and regional facilities). Fold3.com (subscription) holds digitized NARA military records. Louisiana militia records may be at the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Access:** NARA (archives.gov), Fold3.com (subscription, listed in external_links_search results), Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823), and later Lafayette Cemetery (est. 1833). New Orleans uses above-ground tomb burial due to the high water table — a practical necessity that also produced distinctive burial records.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com, listed in external_links_search results) has partial coverage. Physical sexton records for St. Louis cemeteries are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans.
- **Note:** Yellow fever epidemic mortality meant that burial records in peak epidemic years can be voluminous but also chaotic or incomplete.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** New Orleans had active newspapers throughout this period, including the Louisiana Gazette (from 1804), the Louisiana Courier (bilingual French/English), and later the Daily Picayune (from 1837). These carried death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices (including sheriff's sales and succession notices), and runaway enslaved person advertisements.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription, listed in external_links_search results) has some coverage. The Louisiana State Library, the Historic New Orleans Collection, and Tulane University's Howard-Tilton Memorial Library hold physical or microfilm runs of many titles.
- **Content value:** Runaway slave advertisements often include detailed physical descriptions, names, origins, and skills — a major genealogical source for researching enslaved ancestors. Succession notices name heirs. Legal notices can document property disputes.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** The Port of New Orleans was one of the busiest in the US. Passenger manifests (arrival lists) are at NARA and indexed on Ancestry.com. The period 1820 onward saw increasingly systematic manifest requirements under federal law.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists, crew lists, declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (filed in Orleans Parish district courts, pre-1906 in any court of record). Post-1803, immigrants could file declarations in New Orleans courts.
- **Free people of color:** Louisiana had specific documentation requirements for free people of color, including registration papers that functioned as identity documents. These are held at the Louisiana State Archives and Orleans Parish records offices.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered. NARA, the Louisiana State Archives, and Orleans Parish court records are all possible locations.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property tax (assessed at the parish level), personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Territorial and early state tax records survive from the early 1800s.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge; some records at the Louisiana Division of the New Orleans Public Library.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can place a person in Orleans Parish in years between censuses and confirm property ownership.

### Records specific to enslaved and free people of color

This deserves its own entry because New Orleans had an unusually complex tripartite racial structure in the early 1800s:

- **Enslaved people:** Named in succession inventories, notarial acts of sale, manumission acts, runaway advertisements, and (after 1850) federal slave schedules. The New Orleans Notarial Archives is the richest single source for manumissions and individual transactions naming enslaved people.
- **Free people of color:** Had legal standing under Louisiana civil law and generated their own notarial acts, succession records, and property deeds. They appear in the main population schedules of every federal census. The Louisiana Division of the New Orleans Public Library holds significant manuscript collections relating to this community.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (coll. 1612905; indexed + images); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (coll. 1798054; indexed + images); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (coll. 2078341; indexed + images); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (coll. 1543892; index only, no images); Orleans Parish Notarial Acts 1803-1820 (vol. 004990115; browse-only images, French/English) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (all census years for this period); passenger arrival lists; additional Louisiana collections | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Military service records, pension files (NARA-sourced) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions for St. Louis cemeteries and others | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids; some digitized records | Free / Pay-per-view |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume (totalResults: 1) for Orleans Parish, 1800-1850 — the notarial acts volume above, which is the complete result set for that query. `collections_search` returned 4 collections at the Louisiana state level (totalForPlace: 4), which is the complete set returned. These numbers reflect what FamilySearch has indexed or digitized; they are not a measure of what physically survives.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734; the most important physical repository for early New Orleans | In-person in New Orleans; contact for research appointments |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state government records; tax rolls; land records; succession records; free persons of color registrations | In-person; some online finding aids at sos.la.gov |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Church registers not yet microfilmed or digitized; cemetery sexton records | In-person or by correspondence |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) records; court minutes; naturalizations | In-person; some transferred to Louisiana State Archives |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscripts, maps, newspapers; strong on French Quarter and antebellum period | In-person at 533 Royal Street, New Orleans; online finding aids |
| Tulane University Howard-Tilton Memorial Library (Louisiana Collection) | Local histories, genealogical publications, newspaper microfilm | In-person; some digital access |
| Louisiana Division, New Orleans Public Library | Free people of color manuscripts; city directories; newspaper microfilm | In-person; partial online catalog |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal records for Louisiana post-1803; some territorial records | In-person or written request; some records at archives.gov |

---

## Records NOT online

The following categories are known to exist for this period but are not fully (or in some cases at all) available in online databases:

- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (only 167 images spanning 1803-1820 are on FamilySearch; the physical archive holds tens of millions of pages)
- Pre-1837 civil marriage records (before the parish marriage series begins)
- Pre-1819 death records at the civil registration level
- Louisiana State Archives territorial-era government records
- Archdiocese records not yet included in the church records collection
- Free persons of color registration papers
- Tax assessment rolls
- City directories (for locating people between censuses)
- Most newspaper runs (partial coverage on Newspapers.com; physical/microfilm access needed for many titles)

---

## Known record losses — detailed

| Loss event | Date | What was destroyed | Substitute approach |
|---|---|---|---|
| Great Fire of New Orleans | March 1788 | 856 structures; French colonial administrative and church records | Spanish colonial records (which begin 1763) were also damaged; surviving Spanish-era notarial acts and church registers that predate 1788 may exist in Spain (Archivo General de Indias, Seville) |
| Good Friday Fire | December 1794 | Another large section of the city; additional records | Same as above; look for transcriptions made before 1794 |
| Yellow fever epidemics | Ongoing 1800s-1850s | Institutional continuity gaps; death registers can be chaotic in peak years | Cross-check church burial registers against civil death index |
| Flooding/hurricane damage | Periodic | Physical record deterioration | Microfilm copies made before damage may survive at FamilySearch or NARA |
| 1788 pre-period loss effect | — | No colonial vital registers for 1718-1788 at local level | Diocese of Louisiana records may exist in French and Spanish ecclesiastical archives; Archivo General de Indias |

**Key point:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 predate the 1800-1850 research window, but their effect is felt throughout it. People in their 40s, 50s, and 60s in 1820 were born before those fires — their baptismal records, parents' marriage records, and early life documents may simply not exist locally. Researchers must be prepared to look in French and Spanish archives for colonial-era antecedents.

---

## Research tips

- **The notarial records are irreplaceable.** For early New Orleans, a notarial act can substitute for a birth record, marriage certificate, property deed, will, and manumission — all in one document type. Any ancestor who bought or sold property, entered a contract, or had a will drafted went before a notary. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is not optional for serious research here. (Source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Louisiana uses civil law, not common law.** Terms like "succession," "tutorship," and "interdiction" replace "probate," "guardianship," and "conservatorship." Research guides written for common-law states do not transfer directly.
- **Records are in French and Spanish, not just English.** Colonial-era records through roughly the 1820s are predominantly in French. Researchers who cannot read 19th-century French will need a translator or transcription service for the originals. The FamilySearch notarial acts volume (004990115) is in French and English.
- **St. Louis Cathedral registers survive from 1731 with gaps.** This is one of the oldest continuous sacramental series in what is now the United States. For Catholic families, start here before any civil registration source. Check the church records collection (1612905) and contact the Archdiocese Archives for records not yet digitized.
- **Free people of color had a distinct legal status.** They appear in separate registration systems, had the right to hold property and execute notarial acts, and often appear in sources that no other US jurisdiction of this era would have created. The New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division holds key manuscript collections for this community.
- **Search adjoining parishes.** Orleans Parish borders St. Bernard Parish (southeast), Jefferson Parish (west), and St. Tammany Parish (north, across Lake Pontchartrain). Families near these borders generated records on both sides. The Orleans Parish Genealogy wiki page returned only generic content, so neighboring-parish details could not be confirmed from that page — but researchers near the city limits should extend searches to Jefferson and St. Bernard parishes.
- **City directories as census substitutes.** New Orleans had city directories from the 1820s onward. These place individuals at specific addresses in non-census years and are especially valuable between the decennial enumerations. Physical copies are at the Historic New Orleans Collection and the New Orleans Public Library.
- **Look for records in Spain and France for colonial-era ancestors.** The Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain holds records of Spanish colonial Louisiana administration. The Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence, France holds French colonial records. For ancestors whose traces in New Orleans were destroyed in the 1788 or 1794 fires, these are the only recourse.
- **The wiki_place_page tool returned generic content for all four Louisiana research-guide sections** (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) rather than Louisiana-specific articles. Likewise, the constructed-URL wiki_read calls for Louisiana-specific pages (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) all resolved to a generic page. This is a tool coverage gap, not evidence that these wiki pages do not exist. Researchers should visit the FamilySearch Wiki directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for the full text of those articles.

---

There is no `research.json` at the workspace path, so this is a standalone guide and no locality entry is persisted.

---

New Orleans in the early 1800s is a genuinely complex research environment. Three successive colonial regimes (French, Spanish, American) each created their own records in their own languages, and two catastrophic fires before 1800 wiped out much of the French colonial series. What survives is rich but scattered: St. Louis Cathedral baptismal registers from 1731, tens of millions of pages of notarial acts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, Louisiana-level church and probate collections on FamilySearch, federal census records from 1810, and newspaper archives with death notices and legal postings. The single most important warning is that most notarial records — the backbone of early New Orleans research — exist only in person at the Notarial Archives, with just one small digitized volume (167 images, 1803-1820) currently on FamilySearch, and that volume must be browsed image by image with no name index.

The next step is to take these findings and build a targeted research plan: deciding which record types to search first for a specific ancestor, in what order, and at which repositories.

## Boston, Massachusetts — Immigrant Research Guide (1840s)

Here's what the locality-guide agent found for tracing immigrants who entered through the Port of Boston in the 1840s:

---

### Why Boston in the 1840s?

Boston was one of the five primary U.S. ports of entry in the antebellum period and the dominant northeastern port for Irish immigration during the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born. German, English, and Canadian immigrants also arrived in significant numbers.

---

### Key Record Types and Where to Find Them

**1. Passenger Lists (Customs Records) — Start Here**
- **FamilySearch collection 1784312** — "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (~1.2M records). The digitized 1840–1850 volume (image group 003345210) is only **3% name-indexed**, so browsing images is often necessary.
- **Ancestry.com** — Same underlying NARA originals, often more broadly indexed.
- **Physical originals:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) — NARA Record Group 36.
- ⚠️ **Important caveat:** 1840s customs lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — *not* town of origin or family relationships. Expect sparse data.

**2. The Boston Pilot Missing Persons Database — Essential for Irish Ancestors**
- Irish immigrants placed ads in the *Boston Pilot* searching for separated family members, naming the person's **home county or townland in Ireland** — often the most specific geographic data you'll find.
- Freely searchable at **[infowanted.bc.edu](http://infowanted.bc.edu)**, covering 1831–1921.

**3. Catholic Church Records — Critical Before Civil Registration**
- Irish Famine immigrants were overwhelmingly Catholic. The first post-arrival document is usually a **baptism of a Boston-born child or a marriage record**.
- **FamilySearch collection 1921657** — "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (~987K records, images included).
- **Physical records:** Archdiocese of Boston Archives (Brighton, MA) — by appointment.

**4. Naturalization Records**
- **FamilySearch collection 1459213** — ~345K records, indexed and searchable online.
- Pre-1906 papers sometimes record the port and approximate date of arrival — useful for cross-confirming a passenger list entry.
- Courts used: Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas, U.S. Circuit Court, U.S. District Court for Massachusetts.

**5. Vital Records**
- Massachusetts began systematic town-level registration around 1842.
- **FamilySearch collection 2061550** — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (~3.4M records).

**6. Federal Census — The 1850 Census Is Your Anchor Record**
- 1850 was the *first* census to name all household members with ages and birthplaces. An immigrant who arrived in the 1840s and stayed in Boston will be found here with their entire household.
- **1850 Mortality Schedule** covers June 1849–June 1850 — height of Famine arrivals — and records those who died of fever shortly after landing.

**7. Probate Records**
- **FamilySearch collection 1678901** — "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (~567K records). Estate files can establish family relationships and sometimes country of origin.

**8. Military Records**
- Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and Civil War pension files often name birthplace, arrival date, and port — can substitute for a missing passenger list entry.
- **Fold3** (subscription) for indexed service records; NARA for pension files.

**9. Cemetery Records**
- **FindAGrave.com** and **BillionGraves** for headstone transcriptions.
- Major Catholic cemeteries: Holy Cross Cemetery (Malden), St. Augustine Cemetery (South Boston).

---

### Key Physical Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | Original Port of Boston customs passenger lists (RG 36); federal naturalization records (RG 21) |
| **Massachusetts State Archives** | State vital records, court records |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives (Brighton, MA)** | Catholic parish registers from 1840s onward — by appointment |
| **Boston Public Library** | *Boston Pilot* microfilm, local newspapers, city directories |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Specialized Massachusetts collections; AmericanAncestors.org |

1. **Search the passenger list first** — FamilySearch collection 1784312 and Ancestry — but expect name, age, and country only. Browse images; don't rely solely on the index (only 3% indexed for 1840–1850).
2. **For Irish ancestors, search the Boston Pilot database** at infowanted.bc.edu — this is often the *only* source naming a specific county or townland in Ireland.
3. **Check Catholic church records** (FamilySearch 1921657 + Archdiocese of Boston Archives) for baptisms and marriages after arrival.
4. **Pull naturalization papers** — they sometimes include arrival date and port, corroborating the passenger list.
5. **Anchor everything to the 1850 federal census**, which names the whole household.
6. **Variant spellings are common** — Irish and German names were anglicized by customs clerks. Search multiple spellings.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry for Immigrants (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Place:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Role:** One of the five primary U.S. ports of entry in the antebellum period; the dominant northeastern port for Irish immigration during the Great Famine (1845–1852)
- **County seat:** Boston is itself the county seat of Suffolk County
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Population during period:** Boston's population grew rapidly through the 1840s; Wikipedia reports that by 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting the scale of Famine-era arrivals
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, manufacturing, textile industry, construction (fueled in part by immigrant labor)
- **Ethnic composition:** Dominant Irish Catholic wave from 1845 onward; also significant numbers from Germany, England, and Canada
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and other parishes); Protestant denominations (Congregational, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist); Jewish congregations by mid-century
- **Key historical events:** Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) drove mass emigration; Boston received tens of thousands of Famine refugees; immigrants settled densely in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods

## Boundary changes

Suffolk County and its jurisdiction over Boston were stable throughout the 1840s. No boundary changes materially affect which repositories hold records for this period.

## Available record types

### Passenger lists (customs records) — PRIMARY SOURCE

- **Coverage:** 1820–1891
- **What exists:** Customs passenger lists for the Port of Boston, held in National Archives Record Group 36. For 1840s arrivals, entries typically record name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. They do not routinely record town of origin, religion, or family relationships within the same ticket.
- **Digitization:** FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume covering 1840–1850 (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images, 3% name-indexed, full-text searchable). This means the volume can be searched by keyword/full-text but is only 3% name-indexed — a direct surname search in the record index will miss most entries. Budget time to browse images as well.
- **Also indexed on:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection ID 1784312, ~1.2 million records), and Ancestry.com
- **Where originals are held:** National Archives at Boston (located in Waltham, MA) — NARA Record Group 36
- **Critical note:** The volume_search result covers 1840–1850; coverage for later 1840s arrivals through 1865 may be in additional volumes not yet examined. FamilySearch returned 1 total result for this query — check Ancestry's digitized set for broader date coverage within the decade.
- **Content note:** Examine the full manifest for each sailing — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents. A family traveling together appears on the same manifest page.

### Naturalization records

- **Coverage:** 1790–1906 (collection ID 1459213, ~345,000 records)
- **Critical context:** Before 1906, a person could file a declaration of intention ("first papers") and a petition for naturalization in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. Boston immigrants frequently naturalized in the Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas, the U.S. Circuit Court, or the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts.
- **What to expect:** Declaration of intention (sworn 2+ years before petition), petition for naturalization, oath of allegiance. Pre-1906 papers typically record name, country of origin, and sometimes date/port of arrival — the latter can cross-confirm a passenger list entry.
- **Digitization:** FamilySearch collection 1459213 is indexed and searchable online. NARA (Waltham) holds the federal court originals.
- **Repository:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham), Massachusetts State Archives, Suffolk County courthouse records

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Registration level:** Massachusetts began town-level vital registration in 1842. The FamilySearch wiki pages for Massachusetts Vital Records returned a generic fallback rather than Massachusetts-specific content, so I cannot state the statewide registration date from a returned page — verify the exact statewide mandate date at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records).
- **What exists for 1840s Boston:** Town-level birth, marriage, and death records. These would record post-arrival events (children born in Boston, marriages, deaths) — not the immigrant's arrival itself.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection ID 2061550, ~3.4 million records, images included) — indexed and searchable online
- **Repository:** Massachusetts State Archives; also available through FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Gap:** An immigrant who arrived in the 1840s but died or married only after leaving Massachusetts will not appear in Boston's vital records for that later event

### Church records — ESSENTIAL FOR 1840s IMMIGRANTS

- **Why critical:** Catholic parish registers are the primary source for vital events among Irish Famine immigrants, who were overwhelmingly Catholic and arrived before civil registration was comprehensive. The wiki_search result confirms that the Archdiocese of Boston archives holds Catholic parish registers from the 1840s onward, including records of the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (confirming post-arrival children's births), marriages (frequently the first record generated after arrival), burials. Confirmations are a separate dated event — typically several years after baptism — and provide a second dated record for the same individual.
- **Language:** Records are in English (Latin for sacramental formulas)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection ID 1921657, ~987,000 records, images included) — indexed and searchable online
- **Repository:** Archdiocese of Boston Archives (Brighton, MA) for Catholic registers; individual parish offices; FamilySearch microfilm
- **Non-Catholic immigrants:** German Lutheran, Episcopal, Methodist, and Baptist church records are held by respective denominational archives and local congregations. FamilySearch collection 1921657 covers multiple denominations.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1840 (name of household head only, no ages for individuals), 1850 (first census to name all household members with ages and birthplaces — a critical record for 1840s arrivals). 1860 also captures those who arrived and settled.
- **Birthplace column (1850 onward):** Records country of birth, not town or county. An Irish immigrant shows as "Ireland."
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 mortality schedule records deaths in the year June 1849–June 1850, which covers the heaviest Famine arrival period — useful for finding immigrants who died soon after arrival.
- **Digitization:** Federal censuses are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and related databases
- **State census:** Massachusetts did not conduct a state census in this period that fills the 1840s intercensal gap in a meaningful way for immigrant research — the 1850 federal census is the key snapshot

### The Pilot newspaper — "Missing Persons" advertisements

- **What it is:** The Boston Pilot (an Irish Catholic newspaper) published "Missing Persons" advertisements placed by immigrants searching for separated family members. These ads name the person sought, their townland or parish of origin in Ireland, and the inquiring party's Boston address.
- **Coverage:** Especially heavy from 1847 through the 1850s
- **Access:** The Boston College database "A Database of Irish Immigrant Naming" (informally called the "Boston Pilot Missing Persons" database) is freely searchable online at infowanted.bc.edu — this is one of the most specific sources for pinpointing Irish county and townland of origin, which passenger lists do not provide
- **Repository:** Boston College Burns Library; microfilm at various libraries

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories — Suffolk County Probate Court
- **Value for immigrants:** An estate file naming heirs can establish family relationships and sometimes country of origin. Guardianship records name minor children.
- **Coverage:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection ID 1678901, ~567,000 records, images included) — indexed and searchable online
- **Repository:** Suffolk County Probate Court (Boston); Massachusetts State Archives

### Tax records

- **What exists:** Boston city tax records (property and poll tax) from the 1840s. Poll tax lists can place an adult male immigrant in Boston even in years with no other surviving record.
- **Digitization:** Not in FamilySearch's indexed collections for this period based on the tools' results — gap to note
- **Repository:** City of Boston Archives; Massachusetts State Archives

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); many 1840s immigrants later served in the Civil War (1861–1865)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (NARA); Massachusetts state muster rolls (Massachusetts State Archives)
- **Value:** A pension file opened by a veteran or his widow often names birthplace, arrival date, and port — can substitute for a missing passenger list entry
- **Repository:** NARA (Washington, DC and College Park); Fold3 online for indexed service records; Massachusetts State Archives for state militia records

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Holy Cross Cemetery (Malden), St. Augustine Cemetery (South Boston), Old Calvary Cemetery — Catholic cemeteries serving Irish immigrants; also non-sectarian city cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com and BillionGraves provide headstone transcriptions for many Boston-area cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual cemetery offices and the Archdiocese of Boston Archives
- **Value:** A death record from a cemetery may pre-date any civil or church burial record found elsewhere

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Boston Pilot (Irish Catholic, 1838–present); Boston Daily Advertiser; Boston Pilot shipping notices published arrivals
- **Content:** Obituaries (often naming county of origin for Irish immigrants by the 1850s–1860s), marriage notices, legal notices, ship arrival columns
- **Repository:** Boston Public Library (microfilm and digital); Newspapers.com (subscription) for some titles; Boston College Burns Library for Pilot archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts Passenger Lists 1820–1891 (ID 1784312); Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (ID 2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (ID 1921657); Naturalization Records 1790–1906 (ID 1459213); Probate Records 1635–1991 (ID 1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Massachusetts passenger lists (same underlying NARA records, often more fully indexed); U.S. Federal Census; naturalization indexes | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for Record Group 36 (Customs) and RG 21 (Federal Courts) | Free for finding aids; fees for copies |
| Boston Pilot Missing Persons Database (infowanted.bc.edu) | Irish immigrant missing-persons ads 1831–1921 | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery headstone transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Boston newspapers | Subscription |

**Coverage note:** The volume_search returned 1 total digitized volume for Boston 1840–1850 (389 images, 3% name-indexed, full-text searchable). This represents a single microfilm roll — it is almost certainly not the complete run of Port of Boston passenger lists for the decade. The full series is better accessed through FamilySearch collection 1784312 or Ancestry's Massachusetts passenger list collection, which draws on the same NARA originals and applies broader indexing.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston, Waltham MA | Original Port of Boston customs passenger lists (RG 36); federal court naturalization records (RG 21) | In-person; written requests; some records on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | State vital records; state court records; some city/town records | In-person; online catalog at sec.state.ma.us |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives, Brighton MA | Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) from 1840s onward | Written request; appointment |
| Boston Public Library, Boston MA | City directories; Boston Pilot microfilm; local newspapers; map collections | In-person; some digitized |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston MA | Massachusetts genealogical collections; vital records abstracts; city directories | Membership or in-person fee; some online at AmericanAncestors.org |
| Boston City Archives | City tax records; city government records | In-person |
| Suffolk County Courthouse | Probate records; court records | In-person; some on FamilySearch |

## Records NOT online

- Boston city poll and property tax records for the 1840s — not in any indexed online collection based on tool results
- Original ship manifests at NARA Waltham not yet fully digitized beyond the single 1840–1850 volume found in volume_search
- Many individual Catholic parish registers not yet fully digitized — only partially covered by FamilySearch collection 1921657
- Passenger arrival certificates issued to individuals (if any were retained) — physical only

## Known record losses

No major courthouse fire or catastrophic record loss for Suffolk County is documented in the tool results for this period. However:

- Early Boston city vital records prior to systematic town-level registration (which began in Massachusetts around 1842) are sparse — church registers are the primary substitute
- Some Catholic parish registers from the earliest 1840s Boston parishes have gaps or were not systematically kept until congregations stabilized
- The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationally — a significant gap for tracing immigrants who would have been enumerated there after 20 years of residence

## Research tips

- **Start with the passenger list, but expect sparse data.** Customs passenger lists from the 1840s are thinner than later immigration manifests: name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not town of origin or family relationships beyond the manifest page. Use the list to confirm arrival, then pivot to other sources for hometown details. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston))
- **The Boston Pilot Missing Persons database is essential for Irish immigrants.** If your ancestor was Irish and arrived in the 1840s, search infowanted.bc.edu — an ad placed by a relative naming the person's home county or townland in Ireland is often the single most specific record you will find. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston))
- **Catholic church records fill the gap before comprehensive civil registration.** Irish Famine immigrants were Catholic; their first post-arrival document is usually a baptism of a child born in Boston or a marriage record. Search the Archdiocese of Boston Archives and FamilySearch collection 1921657 alongside any civil vital search.
- **Naturalization papers can cross-confirm arrival.** A declaration of intention or petition for naturalization filed in a Boston court often records the port and approximate date of arrival — check FamilySearch collection 1459213 even if you already have a passenger list entry, because the two records together provide corroboration.
- **The 1850 federal census is the anchor record.** It is the first census to name all household members with ages and birthplaces. If your ancestor arrived in the 1840s and stayed in Boston through 1850, the census names the entire household — including children born before emigration who may not appear in any Boston record otherwise.
- **Mortality schedules record early deaths.** The 1850 mortality schedule covers deaths from June 1849 to June 1850 — the height of Famine arrivals. An immigrant who died of fever shortly after landing would appear here.
- **Search across the manuscript pages, not just the index.** Because the one digitized FamilySearch volume is only 3% name-indexed, a name search will miss most entries. When an index search returns nothing, browse the images for the relevant voyage dates. Ship arrival notices in the Boston Daily Advertiser name the vessel and date — use those to target specific manifest pages.
- **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) holds specialized Massachusetts finding aids** not fully replicated on FamilySearch. Their database at AmericanAncestors.org covers some early vital records, city directories, and Boston-area church abstracts.
- **Variant spellings are common.** Irish and German names were anglicized or phonetically respelled by customs clerks. Search under multiple spellings and consider soundex-equivalent variants.

---

This guide covers Boston, Massachusetts as a port of entry for immigrants arriving in the 1840s. The records that survive are strong for that period: FamilySearch has five indexed collections covering passenger lists, vital records, church records, naturalizations, and probate, together running to millions of records. The most important caution is that the customs passenger lists from this decade record very little beyond name, age, and country of origin — so tracing an immigrant back to a specific townland in Ireland or village in Germany almost always requires layering in Catholic church records and, for Irish families, the Boston Pilot Missing Persons database.

The recommended next step is to search FamilySearch collection 1784312 (Massachusetts Passenger Lists, 1820–1891) and Ancestry's corresponding collection for your ancestor's name, keeping in mind variant spellings and the low indexing rate for 1840s manifests — then follow any arrival with a search of the 1850 federal census and FamilySearch collection 1921657 (Massachusetts Church Records) to build out what happened after they landed.

## Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (c. 1830–1907)

### Jurisdiction Overview

Indian Territory was not a U.S. state or territory in the conventional sense — it was federally designated land divided between five tribal governments (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Chickasaw, Seminole) with BIA oversight. **Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until November 16, 1907.** This means the record infrastructure is entirely different from standard U.S. county research — no county clerks, no civil vital registration, no county probate courts for tribal members.

---

### The Most Important Records

#### 1. Dawes Rolls (Final Rolls, 1898–1914) — Start Here
The single most critical resource. Over 101,000 individuals were enrolled as members of the Five Civilized Tribes. Each entry records name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation. Crucially, each person's **enrollment "jacket" file** contains birth, death, and relationship affidavits submitted during enrollment — often the only vital record that exists for a family.
- **FamilySearch:** Collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (ID 1987432), 567,890 records — [search it here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)
- Also indexed on Ancestry.com and Fold3
- **Originals:** NARA Fort Worth (Southwest Region)

> ⚠️ **Freedmen note:** Post–Civil War treaties required each tribe to enroll formerly enslaved Black people as tribal citizens. Dawes Freedmen rolls are a *separate series* — check both "by blood" and Freedmen series for families with mixed African American and Native ancestry.

#### 2. Earlier Rolls (Pre-Dawes, 1830s–1890s)
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — Cherokees who migrated west before main removal
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — Cherokee census in Indian Territory
- BIA annuity payment rolls (who received treaty payments) — function as de facto censuses
- All covered within FamilySearch collection 1987432

#### 3. BIA Agency Records (NARA Record Group 75)
- Held at **NARA Fort Worth** — the primary physical repository for this research
- Includes: annuity rolls, school enrollment, correspondence, census schedules
- Partially microfilmed; most must be accessed physically or via NARA reproduction requests
- Finding aids: [archives.gov/locations/southwest](https://archives.gov/locations/southwest)

#### 4. Treaty Records
- Treaties define who had rights and what records were created
- Full text: **Oklahoma State University Kappler Collection** — [digital.library.okstate.edu/kappler](https://digital.library.okstate.edu/kappler/)
- Treaty negotiations generated commissioner journals and census counts in NARA RG 75

---

### Vital Records (Important Warning)

**No civil vital registration existed in Indian Territory before 1907.** Each tribe had its own government but no civil registration requirement. Oklahoma statewide vital registration began in 1908.

**Substitutes for birth/death records:**
- Dawes enrollment jacket affidavits
- Missionary church registers (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian — active from the 1820s)
- BIA school enrollment records
- FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (ID 1654321)

---

### Other Key Records

| Record Type | What It Covers | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Federal census** | Indian Territory NOT counted until 1900; 1900 + Dawes overlapping is a rich research year | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| **Land/Allotment** | Tribal land → individual allotments under Dawes; no county deed system before 1907 | FamilySearch collection 1541872; NARA Fort Worth |
| **Tribal courts** | Each tribe had its own courts; U.S. District Court at Fort Smith (AR) covered non-citizens | Oklahoma Historical Society; NARA Fort Worth |
| **Civil War military** | Both Union Indian Home Guard and Confederate Indian units; pension files for Union veterans | Fold3.com; NARA Washington, D.C. |
| **Tribal newspapers** | Cherokee Advocate (1844+), Cherokee Phoenix (1828–1834); death/marriage notices | Oklahoma Historical Society; Chronicling America |
| **Removal records** | Emigration rolls from the 1830s removal — establish pre-Oklahoma origins | NARA RG 75 |
| **Guardianship records** | For minor allottees (children with land); rich family data | NARA Fort Worth (U.S. District Court, Indian Territory) |

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Fort Worth** | Dawes originals, enrollment jackets, BIA RG 75, U.S. District Court (IT) records | In-person or reproduction request |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Tribal court records, Five Nations records, territorial newspapers | In-person; some digital finding aids |
| **Cherokee Nation Cultural Resource Center, Tahlequah** | Cherokee tribal records, Cherokee Advocate archives | Contact tribe directly |
| **Other tribal archives** | Each tribe maintains its own archive and citizenship office | Contact each tribe's Cultural Preservation office |
| **FamilySearch** | Rolls (1987432), land (1541872), church records | Free online |
| **Fold3.com** | Civil War Indian regiment service records | Subscription |
| **OSU Kappler Collection** | All U.S.-Indian treaties, full text | Free online |

---

### Known Record Losses
- **Civil War disruption:** The Five Tribes were internally divided 1861–1865; many tribal records from this period are fragmentary or lost
- **1890 federal census:** Largely destroyed in a 1921 fire; Indian Territory wasn't enumerated anyway
- Most BIA agency correspondence and early annuity rolls remain undigitized

---

### Research Tips

1. **Start with Dawes, not vital records** — the enrollment jacket is your birth/death/relationship substitute
2. **Work backwards from Dawes to earlier rolls** — jacket files often cite earlier roll numbers
3. **The tribe matters** — Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole each have distinct record series; identify the tribe first
4. **Search pre-removal states for earlier generations** — adults at removal time were born in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, Mississippi, Alabama, or Florida; their birth and early family records are in those state archives
5. **Watch for dual names** — tribal members often used both English and traditional names; the same person may appear differently in different record series
6. **Check the Arkansas border** — the federal court at Fort Smith (AR) had direct jurisdiction over Indian Territory; families near the border may have records on both sides

---

**Bottom line:** Since there was no civil government in most of Indian Territory before 1907, substitute the Dawes enrollment jacket files and missionary church registers for vital records. Identify which tribe(s) your ancestors belonged to first — that determines which roll series, tribal archive, and record set to target, since each nation kept its own records.
