# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1769/1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Period covered:** French Louisiana (1699–1762), with Spanish overlap from 1762 onward
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (France)
- **Population:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this period; colonial-era census rolls exist at ANOM (France) and partially at the Louisiana Historical Center
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo, tobacco, sugar cane; heavy reliance on enslaved labor; plantation agriculture along the Mississippi
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers, Acadian exiles (from 1755), African enslaved people (brought under the Code Noir from the 1720s), Indigenous peoples, small numbers of German and Swiss colonists
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively under French law; the Code Noir banned other faiths
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Code Noir enacted (Louisiana, 1724); Natchez Massacre (1729); French cession of western Louisiana to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau, 1762); Spanish administration begins (1769); Louisiana Purchase (1803)

## Boundary changes
- 1762: France ceded the western portion (west of the Mississippi) to Spain, and the eastern portion to Britain. Records from 1762 onward may be in Spanish; Spanish administrators continued using French-style notarial records.
- 1800: Spain secretly retroceded to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso).
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase — U.S. sovereignty. Louisiana Territory and, later, the State of Louisiana (1812) succeeded the colonial administration.
- Records created before these transitions stayed in the jurisdiction that created them. Colonial-era records for the Orleans Territory are largely held in New Orleans; records of the broader territory may be in France (ANOM).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed during the French colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Louisiana-specific vital records page, so the statewide civil registration start date cannot be confirmed from tool output. Catholic parish registers are the only vital source for 1699–1812.
- **What exists:** Catholic parish registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials, from 1720 (St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans) onward. These function as birth, marriage, and death records for the period.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral archives (New Orleans); Louisiana Historical Center; partially on FamilySearch (see Church Records below)
- **Gaps:** Records for settlements outside New Orleans may be sparse or lost. The earliest decade (1699–1720) predates organized parish registers.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (French law; other faiths prohibited)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons under Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection ID 1612905) — the date range overlaps the colonial period from 1718
- **Digitized volumes:** FamilySearch volume 004330991 covers "Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803" (264 images). **Digitization level: browse-only. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image. Records are in French and Spanish — original-language reading required.**
- **Additional access:** St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans holds the originals. The Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) holds additional registers.
- **Code Noir records:** Baptism registers of enslaved persons were legally required under the Code Noir — these registers may be the only record naming enslaved individuals in this period.

### Census records
- **Colonial census rolls:** French colonial administrators conducted periodic enumerations. These are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France, and partially at the Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Federal census:** Does not apply to this period. The first federal census covering Louisiana was 1810 (as Orleans Territory, 1810; as Louisiana State, 1820 onward).
- **Access:** ANOM is accessible via correspondence or in-person visit; some rolls have been transcribed and published in local histories. Not available via FamilySearch collections or volumes for this period.

### Probate and court records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection ID 2078341) — the date range begins within the French colonial period (1756)
- **Types:** Estate inventories, successions, guardianships. Under French civil law, probate (succession) proceedings were notarial rather than court-based.
- **Superior Council records:** The Conseil Superieur handled civil and criminal matters, land grants, and estate proceedings. FamilySearch volume 004330992 covers "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), 1699–1769" (149 images). **Digitization level: browse-only. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. In French.**
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system (arpents); Spanish land grants followed similar conventions
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Crown of France (grants called "concessions"), then Spanish Crown. The wiki_search result from FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) notes that French concessions and Spanish land grants are in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office.
- **Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial archive in North America. Public access available.
- **Types:** Concessions (grants), notarial contracts, mortgage records, property transfers
- **Access:** New Orleans Notarial Archives (in-person or correspondence); American State Papers available in print and via HathiTrust digitally; Louisiana State Land Office

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of the Quadruple Alliance (1718–1720), Natchez War (1729–1731), King George's War (1744–1748), Seven Years' War / French and Indian War (1754–1763)
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, officer commissions, pension records for French colonial troops (Compagnies franches de la marine). Militia records.
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France) holds French colonial military records. NARA holds some records for the transition period. Louisiana State Archives may have militia records.
- **Access:** ANOM requires correspondence or in-person visit; some records have been published.

### Cemetery records
- **Access:** Many colonial-era burial records are embedded in the Catholic parish sacramental registers (burial entries), not separate sexton records. St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans (est. 1789) is the oldest extant cemetery.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some entries but colonial-era coverage is limited.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers at St. Louis Cathedral and Louisiana Historical Center.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans (primary colonial port); Mobile (secondary)
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists, colonial muster and settlement rolls. Acadian exile records (1755 deportation from Nova Scotia; many settled in Louisiana from 1764 onward — these are sometimes called "Cajun" ancestry records).
- **Where held:** ANOM (France) holds passenger and settler lists for the French colonial period. NARA has some records for the later territorial period. The Center for Louisiana Studies (University of Louisiana Lafayette) holds Acadian research resources.
- **Acadian records:** The Council for the Development of French in Louisiana (CODOFIL) and the Acadian Memorial (St. Martinville, LA) are specialized repositories for Acadian descent.

### Tax records
- **Colonial period:** No formal American-style tax system existed. Property was assessed through notarial records and succession inventories rather than a separate tax roll series.
- **Substitute value:** Superior Council records and notarial acts serve as the economic-documentation substitute for tax records.

### Newspaper records
- **First Louisiana newspaper:** Le Moniteur de la Louisiane (French-language), founded 1794 — postdates most of the French colonial period.
- **Access:** Louisiana State University (LSU) Hill Memorial Library holds early Louisiana newspaper collections.

| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records, sacramental registers, colonial-era documents | In-person; contact for access |

| Center for Louisiana Studies, UL Lafayette | Acadian and Cajun genealogical resources | In-person and correspondence |
| Acadian Memorial, St. Martinville, LA | Acadian exile records, family histories | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial census rolls (held at ANOM, France) — not digitized on FamilySearch or Ancestry
- French colonial military muster rolls and officer records (ANOM)
- Most original Superior Council court proceedings beyond the FamilySearch browse-only volume

Start at St. Louis Cathedral (1720 onward) and the Louisiana Historical Center. Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result citing https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records
- **Code Noir registers name enslaved persons.** Baptism registers include enslaved people baptized under the Code Noir — often the only documentary evidence of their existence in this period.

The New Orleans Notarial Archives from the 1730s is essential. Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result citing https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants

Which side a settlement was on determines which colonial power's records apply and where those records are held.

Here's the full locality guide the agent produced (saved as **loc_001**) for tracing families in Pennsylvania coal mining towns during the late 1800s:

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Late 1800s Locality Guide

**Core counties covered:** Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland (1860–1900)

---

### Critical Caveats First

1. **No statewide vital registration** existed in Pennsylvania during this period. Birth and death records you'd normally expect from the state simply aren't there. Church registers, mine accident reports, and census mortality schedules carry that weight instead.
2. **Lackawanna County didn't exist until 1878.** Any Scranton-area record before that year is filed under **Luzerne County**.

---

### Key Record Types and Where to Find Them

#### Census Records
- **Federal censuses (1860, 1870, 1880, 1900)** — name, age, birthplace, occupation ("miner," "laborer"), and household members. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1880 census mortality schedule** — lists people who died in the year preceding the census, with cause of death. Vital for a region prone to mine accidents.

#### Church Records (Most Important Vital Source)
The coal region was heavily immigrant — Welsh, Irish, English, Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, German, Italian — each with ethnic parishes. Records are often in the home language.
- **Catholic parishes** — baptisms, marriages, burials. Many microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Welsh Congregational and Baptist churches** — extensive registers for Welsh miners.
- **Protestant denominational archives** — Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Reformed.
- **Where to look:** FamilySearch Catalog (search by county + "church records"), local diocesan archives, and the **Presbyterian Historical Society** in Philadelphia for Presbyterian records.

#### Mine Records
- **Mine accident / coroner's records** — injuries and fatalities were common; coroner's inquests often name the deceased, witnesses, and family.
- **Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines annual reports (1870 onward)** — list fatal accidents by mine and name. Digitized at the **Internet Archive** and **HathiTrust**.
- **Company store ledgers and payroll records** — held by local historical societies or the **Hagley Museum and Library** (Wilmington, DE) for some anthracite firms.

#### Naturalization Records
Most immigrant miners naturalized in the local Court of Common Pleas.
- **Declaration of Intention ("first papers") and Petition for Naturalization** — name, country of origin, sometimes age or arrival date.
- **Where:** County courthouse archives; many microfilmed on FamilySearch. Lackawanna County records at the **Lackawanna County Courthouse**.

#### Land and Tax Records
- **County deed books** — track property ownership; useful when the miner owned a house.
- **County tax lists** — annual lists that can confirm residence and economic status.
- **Where:** County recorder of deeds; many on FamilySearch Catalog.

#### Death and Cemetery Records
- **Pennsylvania did not require statewide death registration until 1906.** Before then, rely on:
  - Church burial registers
  - Cemetery transcriptions (many indexed by DAR, local genealogical societies, or on BillionGraves/FindAGrave)
  - Newspaper death notices (see below)

#### Newspapers
Local papers carried mine accident reports, obituaries, and marriage notices.
- **Key papers:** *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville/Schuylkill Co., 1825–present), *Scranton Republican*, *Wilkes-Barre Record*, *Hazleton Sentinel*.
- **Where:** Chronicling America (Library of Congress) has some; the **State Library of Pennsylvania** (Harrisburg) holds extensive runs; local county libraries often hold originals or microfilm.

#### Immigration and Passenger Records
Most coal region immigrants arrived 1850–1900.
- **Passenger lists** at FamilySearch and Ancestry — key ports were New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore.
- **Castle Garden (pre-1890) and Ellis Island (1892+)** online databases.

#### Social/Fraternal Organization Records
Miners frequently belonged to:
- **Ancient Order of Hibernians** (Irish)
- **Workmen's Benefit Fund / Sons of Italy / Polish National Alliance** — sick/death benefit records sometimes survive with local chapters or at ethnic archives.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Census, church records, naturalizations, some deeds — free |
| **Ancestry** (ancestry.com) | Census, immigration, newspapers, city directories |
| **State Library of Pennsylvania**, Harrisburg | Newspaper runs, Pennsylvania histories |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg | Mine inspection reports, some county records |
| **Hagley Museum and Library**, Wilmington DE | Coal company business records |
| **Lackawanna County Historical Society**, Scranton | Local records, photographs, city directories |
| **Luzerne County Historical Society**, Wilkes-Barre | Same for Luzerne County |
| **Schuylkill County Historical Society**, Pottsville | Schuylkill records, *Miners' Journal* |
| **Balch Institute / Historical Society of Pennsylvania**, Philadelphia | Immigration and ethnic community records |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society**, Philadelphia | Presbyterian church registers statewide |

---

### Recommended Search Order

1. **Census records** — establish the household, birthplaces, and approximate ages.
2. **Church records** — find baptism, marriage, and burial dates once you know the ethnic/religious community.
3. **Naturalization records** — confirm country/region of origin and arrival date.
4. **Passenger lists** — connect to the Old World.
5. **Mine records and newspapers** — fill gaps and find death information pre-1906.

---

The agent noted that a good next step would be building a specific research plan once you have a particular ancestor in mind (e.g., name, approximate dates, county). If you'd like to continue with that, or if you want to dig into any of these record types further, just say the word.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Core counties:** Schuylkill (formed 1811), Luzerne (formed 1786), Lackawanna (formed 1878 from Luzerne), Carbon (formed 1843), Northumberland (formed 1772)
- **County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna), Jim Thorpe/Mauch Chunk (Carbon), Sunbury (Northumberland)
- **Population:** Tool returned no population data for this query; Wikipedia describes dramatic growth driven by immigration from the 1820s onward
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominant; companies maintained employment records alongside civil record system
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish Catholic, Welsh, German, and from the 1880s-1900s: Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, Ukrainian
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), Welsh Congregational/Baptist/Methodist, Lutheran, Reformed, Presbyterian, Orthodox
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials 1875-1877; UMWA founded 1890; Lattimer Massacre 1897

## Boundary changes
- Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne in 1878 — Scranton-area records before 1878 are in Luzerne County
- Carbon County formed from Northampton and Monroe counties in 1843
- Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Northumberland had stable boundaries 1860-1900

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration during 1860-1900; county marriage registration from approximately 1885; statewide death certificates begin 1906 (after target period)
- **What exists:** County marriage registers from ~1885 (FamilySearch collection 1921317, name-indexed); civil births and deaths largely absent
- **Where held:** County courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1921317 online
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, mine accident reports, census mortality schedules

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Irish, Welsh, German, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, Ukrainian
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Diocese of Allentown (Schuylkill, Carbon); Diocese of Scranton (Luzerne, Lackawanna); FamilySearch microfilm
- **Language:** Latin, Welsh, German, Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian

### Census records
- **Federal:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (1890 destroyed); mortality schedules 1860-1880
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct regular state censuses in this period
- **Access:** Indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories
- **Where held:** County courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1999196 (3.2M images, browse-only)
- **Note:** Search administration series — miners often died intestate; guardianship records name surviving minor children

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (state-land state)
- **Where held:** County recorders of deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for original grants
- **Note:** Many miners rented company housing; deed records may be sparse

### Military records
- **Conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865), Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 (subscription); Pennsylvania State Archives

### Mine and occupational records
- **Mine Inspector Reports (from 1870):** List fatal accident victims by name, age, nationality; at Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill 1870-1900 (vol. 002240015):** 410 images, 95% name-indexed, full-text searchable — best-digitized mining volume
- **Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne 1870-1895 (vol. 002240016):** 287 images, browse-only
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna 1878-1900 (vol. 002240017):** 199 images, browse-only
- 23 total matching volumes; only first page of 3 examined

### Cemetery records
- **Online:** FindAGrave, BillionGraves
- **Physical:** Local cemeteries, Historical Society of Schuylkill County

### Newspaper records
- **Key papers:** Miners' Journal (Pottsville), Wilkes-Barre Times, Scranton Tribune
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com; Pennsylvania State Library microfilm

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Ports:** Philadelphia and New York
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests (NARA); county-court naturalizations (pre-1906)
- **Schuylkill County naturalizations 1840s-1906:** Pennsylvania State Archives

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property and personal property lists
- **Substitute value:** Replaces destroyed 1890 census

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1885-1950 (indexed); Probate 1683-1994 (browse-only); Death Certs 1906-1968 (indexed, post-period); Mine Employment Cards Schuylkill (indexed); Mine Accident Reports Luzerne (browse-only); Payroll Ledgers Lackawanna (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1860-1900; immigration/naturalization databases | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Miners' Journal and regional papers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, passenger lists | Free/fee |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Mine Inspector reports; Schuylkill naturalizations; land warrants; military records | In-person/mail |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Mining records, UMWA fragments, cemetery transcriptions | In-person |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton | Mining community and ethnic collections | In-person |
| County Courthouses | Deeds, probate, marriage registers, coroner's inquests, tax records | In-person/mail |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic parish registers for Luzerne/Lackawanna | Written request |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill/Carbon | Written request |
| NARA Philadelphia | Regional naturalization records | In-person/mail |

## Records NOT online
- Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne (browse-only images, no index)
- Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna (browse-only images, no index)
- County tax records (physical at courthouses)
- Coroner's inquest files (physical at courthouses)
- UMWA membership rolls (fragmentary, physical at historical societies)
- Pre-1885 marriage records (church registers, largely microfilm or physical)
- Ethnic press in Polish/Lithuanian/Slovak/Ukrainian (not in major online databases)

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census destroyed nationwide (1921 fire)
- No catastrophic courthouse fire confirmed for major coal-region courthouses

## Research tips
- Identify the specific ethnic parish before searching Catholic records
- Lackawanna records before 1878 are in Luzerne County
- Mine Inspector annual reports (1870+) are a unique death register for miners
- Naturalization before 1906 filed in any court; check county Court of Common Pleas
- Tax lists 1889-1891 substitute for missing 1890 census
- 1880 and 1900 census schedules record birthplace of parents and year of immigration
- FamilySearch wiki Pennsylvania-specific pages returned generic content; visit wiki directly

output.text_response:
Here's the full locality guide the agent produced:

---

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, Early Puritan Settlement (1620–1700)

## Critical jurisdiction split

**Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691) are entirely separate research territories.** They had separate courts, churches, and record systems. A family at Plymouth in 1650 left no trace in Massachusetts Bay records, and vice versa. They merged in 1691 into the Province of Massachusetts Bay.

---

## Best record types for this period

### 1. Town Vital Records (from 1639)
Massachusetts Bay mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths in 1639 — the earliest civil registration in the colonies. Start with:
- **FamilySearch collection 2061550** — *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (~3.4M records, name-indexed, free)
- **Tanner–Corbin "Vital Records of [Town] to 1850" published series** — abstracts 200+ towns; widely held at libraries and on FamilySearch

### 2. Congregational Church Records
Before 1639, church baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary proceedings are the primary source. Church discipline records name people in ways no civil source does.
- **FamilySearch collection 1921657** — *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (~987K records, partly indexed)
- **Digitized volume 007612045** — Suffolk County Congregational admissions & baptisms, 1630–1700 (121 images, 0% name-indexed but **full-text searchable**)
- Colonial Society of Massachusetts has published many individual church registers

### 3. Probate Records
Estate inventories from this era are extraordinarily detailed — listing every belonging, debt, and creditor, often naming children and neighbors.
- **FamilySearch collection 1678901** — *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (~567K records, name-indexed)
- County probate courts hold originals; many are microfilmed

### 4. Town Meeting & Proprietors' Records
The founding land proprietors of each town are listed formally, and town meeting minutes name all property owners.
- **Digitized volume 007612044** — Town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620–1698 (188 images, browse only — no keyword search)

### 5. Plymouth Colony Published Records
Nathaniel Shurtleff's *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (12 vols., 1855–1861) transcribes court, vital, and other Plymouth Colony records in full. Available on archive.org and through NEHGS.

### 6. The Great Migration Study Series (NEHGS)
Robert Charles Anderson's *The Great Migration Begins* (3 vols.) documents every known settler who arrived 1620–1643, with full sources. **This is the single most important research tool for this period.** If your ancestor came in the Great Migration wave, start here.

---

## Key repositories

| Repository | What's there |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (free) | Town vitals, church records, probate — see collections above |
| **NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org** (subscription) | Manuscript collections, Great Migration series, *New England Historical & Genealogical Register* |
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | Colony-level records 1620–1691; land grants before 1643; General Court; militia; governor's correspondence |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Deeds from 1643 (when counties formed); earlier land grants are at the Massachusetts Archives |
| **The National Archives, Kew (UK)** | English port departure records for Great Migration voyagers |
| **FindAGrave** | Some colonial-era headstones (stone survival from 1620s–1650s is sparse) |

---

## Gaps and cautions

- **No federal census before 1790.** Use tax rate lists, militia muster rolls, and proprietors' lists as substitutes to place a person in a town in a given year.
- **No newspapers before 1704.** The *Boston News-Letter* began 1704; ignore newspaper databases for this period.
- **Metacom's War (King Philip's War, 1675–1676)** destroyed ~12–13 towns. If your ancestor was in Deerfield, Brookfield, Medfield, or similar communities, town records may be lost — shift to colony-level court and probate records.
- **Old-Style calendar dates.** The year began March 25. "10 February 1648" in an original record = February 1649 in modern reckoning. Transcriptions often show this as "1648/9."
- **FamilySearch passenger list collection 1784312 starts in 1820** — do not use it for colonial research.
- **Puritan naming patterns:** Old Testament names repeat heavily across generations (Ebenezer, Mehitable, Increase, Experience, Thankful). Do not assume uniqueness from a given name alone — always distinguish by age, spouse, and location.

---

## Suggested starting path

1. Identify the specific **town** your ancestor lived in (not just "Massachusetts").
2. Search **FamilySearch collection 2061550** by name for town vital records.
3. Pull the **Tanner–Corbin published volume** for that town for the same period.
4. If the ancestor arrived 1620–1643, consult the **Great Migration series** (NEHGS).
5. If Plymouth Colony, use **Shurtleff's 12-volume published records**.
6. For pre-1643 records or anything not found at the county level, go to the **Massachusetts Archives**.

All substantive Massachusetts-specific content came from the `wiki_search` and Wikipedia results. Here is the guide.

---

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700, Early Puritan Settlement)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Two separate colonial jurisdictions existed simultaneously and must be treated as distinct research territories:
  - Plymouth Colony (1620–1691): founded by Separatists (Pilgrims) at Plymouth; merged into Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1691.
  - Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628/1630–1691): founded by Puritan migrants under Governor John Winthrop; became the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **Administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; after 1691, Province of Massachusetts Bay under royal charter
- **Population during period:** No colonial census population data was returned by tools. Governor Winthrop's Great Migration brought approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640 (per Wikipedia's Massachusetts Bay Colony article). The total English colonial population was very small before 1630 and grew throughout the century.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fishing, fur trade, timber; small farming towns with communal land grants
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Protestant migrants; small numbers of Dutch traders; Indigenous Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc, Narragansett, and other peoples (whose records are almost entirely absent from colonial documentation)
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church of Massachusetts Bay; Separatist Congregational at Plymouth; Quakers arrived by the 1650s and were actively persecuted; Anglicans present in small numbers
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630–1643; Pequot War 1636–1638; settlement of Rhode Island 1636 (dissenters expelled from Massachusetts Bay); Metacom's War (King Philip's War) 1675–1676, which destroyed many towns and disrupted record-keeping; Salem witch trials 1692

## Boundary changes

- **Critical split:** Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691) were entirely separate jurisdictions with separate record systems. A family in Plymouth in 1650 was NOT in Massachusetts Bay — their records are in Plymouth Colony sources, not Massachusetts Bay sources. Search both.
- **Merger:** In 1691, both colonies merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay. After 1691, one administrative structure applies.
- **County formation:** Massachusetts Bay created its first four counties — Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, and Hampshire — in 1643. Probate, land, and court records filed from 1643 onward are at the county level. Records before 1643 (1630–1643) were kept at the colony level only.
- **Plymouth Colony counties:** Plymouth, Barnstable, and Bristol counties were created within Plymouth Colony. Their records are published and held separately (see below).
- **Maine:** Much of modern Maine was part of Massachusetts until 1820; Massachusetts records sometimes include Maine families.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1639 — this is colonial-era registration, not statewide civil registration. Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1842 in Massachusetts. The FamilySearch Wiki's specific Massachusetts Vital Records page did not return in this survey (redirected to a generic page), so the exact mandate wording could not be confirmed; the 1639 date comes from the Wikipedia article on Massachusetts Bay Colony.
- **What exists:** Town clerk vital records (births, marriages, deaths) from approximately 1639 onward, town by town. Survival rate is high but not universal — some early registers were lost. Plymouth Colony has separately published vital records.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices hold the originals. The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" published series (Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts over 200 Massachusetts towns and is widely available in libraries and on FamilySearch. FamilySearch collection **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (collection ID 2061550, ~3.4 million records) is name-indexed and available free at FamilySearch.org.
- **Gaps:** Plymouth Colony before 1643 has sparse civil recording; rely on church records and published transcriptions. Many events before 1639 were not recorded at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; Mayflower passenger records; "Great Migration" study series.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational (dominant, both Puritan and Separatist); Quakers (from 1650s); Anglican (sparse before 1700)
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Disciplinary records name individuals in ways no other source does.
- **Where held:** Many early Congregational registers have been published by the Colonial Society of Massachusetts and local historical societies. FamilySearch collection **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (collection ID 1921657, ~987,000 records) is name-indexed. Two digitized volumes were found in volume search:
  - Volume 007612045 (121 images): Congregational church admissions and baptisms, Suffolk County, 1630–1700. This volume is 0% name-indexed but is **full-text searchable** (not browse-only — you can keyword-search it via FamilySearch's fulltext search interface).
- **Language:** English. Latin was not used in Congregational registers (unlike Anglican and Catholic churches).
- **Note:** Church records at Plymouth Colony often contain family groupings (baptism entries listing parents' names) that can substitute for missing vital records.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census was 1790 — entirely outside this period.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No colonial census or systematic head-of-household count for Massachusetts Bay or Plymouth Colony was returned by the tools. There is no equivalent to a census for this period.
- **Substitutes:** Tax lists, militia muster rolls, proprietors' lists, and town meeting records functioned as de facto population enumerations. See "Town meeting and proprietors' records" below under Digitized Volumes.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships. Estate inventories from this period are extraordinarily detailed — they list every household object, animal, and debt — and are among the richest family history sources of the era.
- **Date range:** Massachusetts Bay probate begins 1635 at the county level (after counties were formed in 1643; the earliest colony-level records predate 1643 and are at the Massachusetts Archives). Plymouth Colony probate begins in the 1620s and is published in Nathaniel Shurtleff's *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England* (12 volumes).
- **Where held:** County probate courts hold the originals. FamilySearch collection **Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991** (collection ID 1678901, ~567,000 records) is name-indexed. Essex County probate records are particularly well preserved and indexed.
- **Court records:** The General Court (colonial legislature/supreme court) records for Massachusetts Bay are at the Massachusetts Archives. Court of Assistants records document criminal proceedings. These name ordinary colonists in many contexts beyond lawsuits.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (not rectangular survey — Massachusetts is a state-land state, not a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors granted land from the colony-level grant. Individual deeds were recorded at county registries of deeds after 1643. Before 1643, land grants were colony-level records held at the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' grants, deeds, mortgages. Town meeting records contain proprietors' (founding land-grantee) lists that name every original settler of a town.
- **Digitized volume:** Volume 007612044 (188 images): Town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620–1698. This volume is 0% name-indexed and **not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds hold originals; Massachusetts Archives holds colony-level grants.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War 1636–1638; Metacom's War (King Philip's War) 1675–1676; various skirmishes with French Canada after 1680.
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, colony pay lists, grant records for service, veterans' lists. The Massachusetts Bay Colony maintained a general militia requiring all able-bodied men.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives holds colonial militia records. Published transcriptions exist (e.g., *The Soldiers in King Philip's War* by George Bodge). NARA holds no 17th-century Massachusetts military records — this predates federal record-keeping.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Granary Burying Ground (Boston, from 1660), King's Chapel Burying Ground (Boston, from 1630), Copp's Hill (Boston, from 1659), Old Burial Hill (Plymouth, from 1620). Many town burying grounds were established with the towns themselves.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) covers many colonial-era stones, but stone survival from the 1620s–1650s is sparse — wooden markers were common.
- **Physical records:** Early sexton records rarely survive before 1700. Headstone inscriptions are the primary cemetery source.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The first newspaper in the colonies was *Publick Occurrences Both Forreign and Domestick* (Boston, 1690, suppressed after one issue). The *Boston News-Letter* began 1704 — outside this period.
- **Coverage gap:** No regular newspapers existed in Massachusetts before 1700. This record type is not applicable to the 1620–1700 period.

### Immigration and emigration records (passenger lists)

- **Relevant ports:** Southampton and Bristol (England) for departure; Boston, Salem, Plymouth, and other Massachusetts Bay ports for arrival.
- **Record types:** English port departure records (some survive at The National Archives, Kew, UK); colonial customs records; ship journals. The most complete source for 1620–1643 arrivals is the New England Historic Genealogical Society's "Great Migration" study series, which documents every known settler who arrived 1620–1643 with full citation.
- **Where held:** English departure records at The National Archives (UK). For arrivals, the Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (collection ID 1784312) does **not** cover the colonial period — its date range starts 1820. This collection is not applicable to this research period.
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests were not systematically maintained by colonial authorities in the modern sense. Family units are best reconstructed through the "Great Migration" series and church admission records, not formal manifests.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Colony tax rates (levies assessed on towns), town rates (assessed on individuals within towns).
- **Date range:** Colony rates from the 1630s onward survive in General Court records.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives. Some have been published by NEHGS.
- **Substitute value:** Town rate lists name male householders and can substitute for the absent census in locating a person in a specific town in a specific year.

### Probate and court records (colony level)

Plymouth Colony's court and vital records were published in full in Nathaniel Shurtleff's *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (12 vols., 1855–1861), available digitally via archive.org and through NEHGS. These are indexed and among the most thoroughly published colonial records in North America.

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Every Massachusetts Bay town held formal town meetings recorded by a town clerk. These minutes name every property owner and many other residents in the context of road maintenance, poor relief, fence viewers, and local governance. They are a genealogical source of first importance and are partly captured in the digitized volume 007612044 (browse-only).
- **Proprietors' records:** The founding land proprietors of each town were listed in a formal register. These are the earliest name lists for each community.
- **Published local and county histories:** 19th-century town histories (e.g., Lucius Paige's *History of Cambridge*, Joseph Felt's *Annals of Salem*) frequently reprint 17th-century vital records, church records, and name lists now lost in original form. These are irreplaceable.
- **Great Migration Study Series (NEHGS):** Robert Charles Anderson's *The Great Migration Begins* (3 vols.) and the ongoing *Great Migration* series document every known settler 1620–1643 with sources — this is the single most important research tool for this period.

---

## Digitized volumes (FamilySearch) — complete result set

Volume search returned exactly 2 volumes (totalResults: 2) for Massachusetts 1620–1700. Both are detailed below — this is the complete set, not a truncated page.

| Volume ID | Images | Record Type | Coverage | Indexed? | Full-text? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 007612044 | 188 | Town meeting and proprietors' records | Massachusetts, 1620–1698 | 0% | No — browse only |
| 007612045 | 121 | Congregational church admissions and baptisms | Suffolk County, MA, 1630–1700 | 0% | Yes — full-text searchable |

Both volumes have 0% name-indexing. Volume 007612044 must be browsed image by image with no search capability. Volume 007612045 can be keyword-searched via FamilySearch's full-text search despite not being name-indexed.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (coll. 2061550, ~3.4M records); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (coll. 1921657, ~987K records); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (coll. 1678901, ~567K records); 2 digitized browse/full-text volumes | Free |
| Ancestry | Massachusetts collections (specific titles not returned by tools) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery and headstone records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Colonial-era Massachusetts records are sparse here; mainly applicable post-1790 | Free/in-person |

**Coverage note:** The `external_links_search` returned 6 results but they were generic (Ancestry census, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA, FamilySearch Wiki vital records category) — none Massachusetts-specific or colonial-specific. The `totalForPlace` figure was not disaggregated by place, so the extent of FamilySearch's curated Massachusetts-specific external links could not be confirmed from this tool run.

**FamilySearch passenger lists collection 1784312 (1820–1891) does NOT apply to this period** and should not be used for 1600s research.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Colony-level records 1620–1691; General Court records; probate before county formation; militia records; land grants; governor's correspondence | In-person; some records on microfilm through NEHGS and FamilySearch |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical research library in New England; manuscript collections; published genealogies; Great Migration study series; Tanner–Corbin vital records series | In-person (members); online subscription (AmericanAncestors.org) |
| County Registries of Deeds (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Hampshire, Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol) | Deeds and land records from county formation dates (1643 for first four counties) | In-person; some microfilm at FamilySearch |
| County Probate Courts | Estate files from county formation onward | In-person; many microfilmed by NEHGS and FamilySearch |
| Plymouth County Registry of Deeds / Massachusetts Archives | Plymouth Colony original records (1620–1691) | In-person; published in Shurtleff's 12-volume set |
| The National Archives (Kew, UK) | English port departure records; Crown correspondence with colonial governors | In-person (UK) or document ordering service; some digitized on Ancestry UK |
| Colonial Society of Massachusetts | Published Congregational church records | Library access; publications widely held |

---

## Records NOT online

- Pre-1643 colony-level land grants and court records (Massachusetts Archives — physical access or microfilm)
- Town rate lists (tax records) — mostly physical at Massachusetts Archives or in published transcriptions
- Militia muster rolls and pay lists for Metacom's War and other conflicts — physical at Massachusetts Archives
- Most individual Congregational church registers from specific towns not yet captured in collection 1921657
- Early town meeting minutes not captured in volume 007612044
- English departure records for the Great Migration (The National Archives, Kew)

---

## Known record losses

- **Metacom's War (King Philip's War), 1675–1676:** Approximately 12–13 Massachusetts towns were completely destroyed, including Deerfield, Brookfield, and Medfield. Town clerk records for those communities were lost or severely disrupted. If your ancestor was in an affected town, shift to colony-level court records, probate, and neighboring-town church records for the mid-1670s gap.
- **General attrition:** Wooden markers, damp storage, and early-period neglect means some town registers from the 1630s–1650s are fragmentary. The Tanner–Corbin published series and NEHGS manuscript holdings represent the best surviving transcriptions.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with the Great Migration series.** Robert Charles Anderson's *The Great Migration Begins* (NEHGS) documents every known settler who arrived in Massachusetts 1620–1643. If your ancestor arrived in this wave, this series is the first stop — it aggregates all surviving sources. Source: wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Treat Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay as entirely separate research territories.** Records, courts, church structures, and probate systems were independent until 1691. A settler at Plymouth in 1630 left no trace in Massachusetts Bay records. Source: Wikipedia Plymouth Colony article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_Colony).
- **Search at the town level, not the county level, for vital records.** Massachusetts Bay mandated town-level recording in 1639. The Tanner–Corbin published series (Vital Records of [Town] to 1850) is organized town by town and is the standard starting point after FamilySearch collection 2061550. Source: wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records
- **Congregational church records are the primary source before 1639 and a critical supplement afterward.** Church admissions, baptisms, and disciplinary records name people in contexts no civil record does. Volume 007612045 on FamilySearch covers Suffolk County Congregational admissions and baptisms 1630–1700 and is full-text searchable. The Colonial Society of Massachusetts has published many more registers. Source: wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational
- **Use the Massachusetts Archives for 1630–1643.** County-level records did not exist before 1643. All probate, land, and court matters before that date were handled at the colony level and are at the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Probate estate inventories from this period are unusually rich.** They list every belonging, debt, and creditor, sometimes naming children, neighbors, and business associates. Even intestate administrations often include family testimony identifying heirs.
- **Check neighboring colonies.** Roger Williams expelled from Massachusetts Bay in 1636 founded Providence (Rhode Island). Anne Hutchinson's followers founded Portsmouth, Rhode Island, in 1638. Many families moved between Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut. A disappearance from Massachusetts records may mean a move to a neighboring colony, not a death.
- **Old-style vs. new-style calendar dates.** Before 1752, England and its colonies used the Julian calendar with the year starting March 25 (Lady Day). A date written as "10 February 1648" in an original record is February 1649 by modern reckoning. Transcriptions often write this as "1648/9." Be precise when searching and recording dates.
- **Naming patterns:** Puritan naming strongly favored Old Testament names (Ebenezer, Increase, Mehitable, Thankful, Experience, Preserved, Resolved). The same name often repeated across generations. Do not assume a unique individual from a given name alone — distinguish by age, spouse, and location.
- **NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org)** is the essential subscription database for this period, complementing FamilySearch. It holds manuscript collections, family databases, and the full run of the *New England Historical and Genealogical Register* — the oldest genealogical journal in America, running since 1847.

---

**Note on wiki pages:** All four `wiki_place_page` sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and all six constructed-URL `wiki_read` calls redirected to a generic "Genealogy Records" page rather than Massachusetts-specific content. The Massachusetts-specific material in this guide comes from `wiki_search` results (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational) and Wikipedia. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy for updated locality-specific guidance.

---

This guide covers Massachusetts from 1620 to 1700, the era of the Puritan and Pilgrim settlements. The two colonial jurisdictions — Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony — each kept their own records until 1691, when they merged. The most important surviving records from this period are: (1) town vital records mandated from 1639, widely indexed on FamilySearch; (2) Congregational church registers, partly digitized and some full-text searchable; (3) probate estate inventories, highly detailed and partly indexed on FamilySearch; (4) town meeting and proprietors' records, digitized but browse-only; and (5) the published Plymouth Colony records and the Great Migration study series, which are the researcher's most important guides. The biggest warnings are the calendar date ambiguity (Julian vs. Gregorian calendar, year beginning March 25), the complete separation of Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay records before 1691, and the record losses from Metacom's War in the mid-1670s.

The logical next step is to identify the specific town or county your ancestors lived in, then pull the relevant town vital records volume from the Tanner–Corbin series and search FamilySearch collection 2061550 by name — those two searches together cover the most accessible portion of the surviving record base.

**Oklahoma & Indian Territory — Land Run Era (c. 1880–1910)**
*(Locality entry saved as `loc_001`)*

---

### Key Jurisdiction Split to Understand First

Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory were **two separate jurisdictions** until statehood in 1907. They kept records in different systems and those records now sit in different archives. Before you search, establish which side of the line your ancestor was on — it determines everything else.

---

### Most Valuable Record Classes

#### 1. Federal Homestead & Land Records
- **What:** Land Run claims, homestead entries, original land patents
- **Where:** NARA (partially name-indexed on FamilySearch; bulk at National Archives)
- **Notes:** The 1889 Land Run opened the Unassigned Lands; look for the original entry case files, which can include affidavits, contestant hearings, and proof of settlement

#### 2. County Marriage Records (from 1890)
- **Where:** FamilySearch (indexed), county courthouses, Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)
- **Notes:** Counties were created quickly after the Land Run; check which county your ancestor's township fell under — boundaries shifted

#### 3. Dawes Commission Enrollment Records (Indian Territory families)
- **Indexed collection:** "Indian Censuses and Rolls" — FamilySearch collection 1987432 — start here to get a Dawes Roll number
- **Enrollment jackets (case files):** FamilySearch vol. 005221389 — **browse-only** (not name-indexed, not full-text searchable); use the Roll number from the indexed collection to find the right jacket
- **What's inside:** Family statements, witness testimony, blood-degree determinations — rich genealogical detail

#### 4. 1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census
- **Where:** Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS), Oklahoma City
- **Why critical:** The national 1890 federal census was destroyed in a 1921 fire. Oklahoma Territory's special census is one of the only surviving 1890 census-era records *anywhere in the U.S.* — a major find for anyone with Oklahoma Territory ancestors

#### 5. Federal Census Records
- **1900, 1910** cover post-Land Run settlement; 1900 is especially useful for establishing who had arrived and where they were by then
- **Indian Territory schedules** are separate from Oklahoma Territory schedules; FamilySearch has both

#### 6. Vital Records (State-level)
- Oklahoma didn't mandate statewide birth/death registration until **1908** (one year after statehood)
- County-level records predate this; coverage is uneven
- **Verify current start dates** at: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records

#### 7. Church Records
- Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian missions were active in Indian Territory before the Land Run; mission records may predate any civil registration
- OHS holds many of these

#### 8. Probate Records
- Filed in district courts; OHS and county courthouses hold original records
- Especially useful for identifying heirs and property chains after a settler died

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)**, Oklahoma City | Territorial records, 1890 special census, church records, early county records, newspapers |
| **NARA — Southwest Region (Fort Worth, TX)** | Federal homestead case files, federal court records for Indian Territory, Dawes files |
| **FamilySearch** | Indexed marriage, census, and vital records; Dawes roll indexes; some county records |
| **Five Civilized Tribes Records at Muskogee** (NARA branch) | Records specific to Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole nations |

---

### Practical Notes from the Agent

- **The 1890 OHS special census is a rare survivor** — search it first for Oklahoma Territory ancestors
- **Dawes enrollment:** Start with the indexed collection (1987432) → get a Roll number → then browse the jacket volume (005221389) for the case file
- The wiki pages for Oklahoma-specific record types returned generic fallback content during this search; the dates and details above come from wiki search results and Wikipedia. Confirm civil registration start dates directly at the FamilySearch Oklahoma wiki once accessible.

The full homestead case file at NARA (RG 49) contains witness testimony naming neighbors and family members; the BLM GLO patent record alone does not.

Most 1889 Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, or other Midwestern/Southern states — trace backward to the departure state for earlier vital, land, and court records.

When Oklahoma became a state in 1907, Indian Territory county records were absorbed into eastern Oklahoma counties; search both the pre-1907 territorial series at NARA Fort Worth and the post-1907 county courthouse for events straddling statehood.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Oklahoma, United States (1880-1910, focused on the 1889 Land Run and territorial period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory formally established May 2, 1890; statehood November 16, 1907
- **Administrative centers:** Guthrie (territorial capital); land offices at Guthrie and Kingfisher
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government (General Land Office / Department of Interior) for territorial records
- **Economy:** Homestead farming, cattle ranching, small-town mercantile trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Midwest/South; African American freedmen communities; Five Civilized Tribes in Indian Territory
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Christian/Disciples of Christ (post-1889); mission churches in Indian Territory from 1820s
- **Key events:** Land Run April 22, 1889; subsequent runs 1891-1895; Dawes Commission enrollment 1898-1906; statehood 1907

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889: Unassigned Lands were federal territory with no county structure; Indian Territory separately governed
- May 2, 1890: Oklahoma Territory created with seven counties
- 1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged into state; 75 initial counties formed
- Records from Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory are in different federal and state series

## Available record types

### Land records
- FamilySearch: Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907 (coll. 1541872, 234,567 records, indexed + images)
- FamilySearch digitized volume 005221388: 402 images of 1889-1907 homestead final proofs, 74% name-indexed
- BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov): land patents searchable by name, free
- Originals: NARA Washington D.C., Record Group 49

### Vital records
- No statewide civil registration during territorial period (1890-1907)
- County marriage records from county formation: Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995 (coll. 2134789, 456,789 records, indexed + images)
- Statewide birth/death registration began 1908 (post-statehood)
- Pre-registration alternatives: church records, newspaper notices, territorial court records

### Indian Territory vital and enrollment records
- Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959 (coll. 1987432, 567,890 records, indexed + images)
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets: FamilySearch vol. 005221389, 176 images, BROWSE-ONLY (0% indexed)

### Church records
- Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965 (coll. 1654321, 123,456 records, indexed + images)
- Post-1889 local church registers largely physical at churches or denominational archives

### Census records
- 1890 federal census destroyed; Oklahoma Territory 1890 Special Census at Oklahoma Historical Society
- 1900 and 1910 federal censuses: indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- Dawes Rolls function as census equivalent for Indian Territory residents

### Probate and court records
- Oklahoma Territory district court records at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives
- Include probate, naturalization, civil and criminal cases
- Largely physical only

### Military records
- Service records, pensions: NARA Washington; Fold3 (subscription)
- Spanish-American War (1898) territorial troops

### Cemetery records
- FindAGrave: broad Oklahoma coverage, free
- Physical sexton records at counties, municipalities, local churches

### Newspaper records
- Newspapers.com (subscription); Library of Congress Chronicling America (free, partial)
- Homestead final proof legal notices published in territorial papers

### Immigration and naturalization
- Territorial court naturalizations at NARA Fort Worth (pre-1906)
- Federal district court naturalizations post-1906
- Passenger manifests on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Tax records
- County tax rolls from 1890 onward; substitute for destroyed 1890 federal census
- Physical at county courthouses and Oklahoma State Archives

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 4 indexed collections; 2 digitized volumes | Free |
| BLM GLO Records | Land patents | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1900, 1910; Oklahoma collections | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Oklahoma newspapers 1889+ | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Partial territorial newspaper digitization | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Fort Worth, TX | District court, Dawes Commission, probate, naturalization | In-person / mail |
| NARA Washington D.C. | GLO records, homestead case files | In-person / mail |
| Oklahoma State Archives | Territorial and state records | In-person / mail |
| Oklahoma Historical Society | 1890 territorial census, newspapers, manuscripts | In-person / some digital |
| County courthouses | Deeds, marriages, probate, tax | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial district court case files
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (browse-only, no index)
- County tax rolls 1890-1899
- 1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census (largely physical)
- Early post-1889 church registers
- Rejected homestead application files

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census destroyed 1921; Oklahoma Territory Special Census at OHS is a critical substitute
- Some early county courthouse records lost to fire or flood; verify county-by-county

## Research tips
- Start with the full homestead case file at NARA, not just the BLM patent record
- Determine Oklahoma Territory vs. Indian Territory jurisdiction before searching archives
- Search territorial newspapers for homestead final proof legal notices
- Trace backward to departure states (Kansas, Texas, Missouri) for pre-1889 records
- For possible tribal members, start with FamilySearch collection 1987432 (indexed Dawes Rolls)
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census at OHS is one of the few surviving 1890-era enumerations nationally

**Wiki coverage gap:** All four FamilySearch wiki_place_page sections for Oklahoma returned only a generic fallback guide rather than Oklahoma-specific content, and the six constructed-URL wiki reads (Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate, Census, Oklahoma Genealogy) all redirected to the same generic page. ---

The survey covers Oklahoma and Indian Territory from roughly 1880 to 1910, centered on the 1889 Land Run. The most important record classes for this period are federal homestead files (partly name-indexed on FamilySearch and fully documented at NARA), county marriage records (indexed on FamilySearch from 1890), the Dawes Commission enrollment records for Indian Territory families, and the 1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census at the Oklahoma Historical Society — which is one of the only surviving census-era records from 1890 anywhere in the country, since the national federal census was destroyed in 1921. The 1890 federal census was destroyed nationally in 1921; the Oklahoma Territory 1890 Special Census at the Oklahoma Historical Society is one of the few surviving 1890-era enumerations in the nation.
Homestead claimants were required by federal law to publish notice of final proof in a local newspaper — search territorial newspaper legal notices as a direct companion to homestead case files.
The full homestead case file at NARA (RG 49) contains witness testimony naming neighbors and family members; the BLM GLO patent record alone does not.
Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (FamilySearch vol. 005221389) are browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; they must be browsed image by image.
Naturalizations before September 27, 1906 were filed in any court of record including territorial district courts; NARA Fort Worth holds Oklahoma Territory district court records.
Most 1889 Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, or other Midwestern/Southern states — trace backward to the departure state for earlier vital, land, and court records.

When Oklahoma became a state in 1907, Indian Territory county records were absorbed into eastern Oklahoma counties; search both the pre-1907 territorial series at NARA Fort Worth and the post-1907 county courthouse for events straddling statehood.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma, United States (1880-1910, focused on the 1889 Land Run and territorial period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory formally established May 2, 1890; statehood November 16, 1907
- **Administrative centers:** Guthrie (territorial capital); land offices at Guthrie and Kingfisher
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government (General Land Office / Department of Interior) for territorial records
- **Economy:** Homestead farming, cattle ranching, small-town mercantile trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Midwest/South; African American freedmen communities; Five Civilized Tribes in Indian Territory
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Christian/Disciples of Christ (post-1889); mission churches in Indian Territory from 1820s
- **Key events:** Land Run April 22, 1889; subsequent runs 1891-1895; Dawes Commission enrollment 1898-1906; statehood 1907

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889: Unassigned Lands were federal territory with no county structure; Indian Territory separately governed
- May 2, 1890: Oklahoma Territory created with seven counties
- 1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged into state; 75 initial counties formed
- Records from Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory are in different federal and state series

## Available record types

### Land records
- FamilySearch: Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907 (coll. 1541872, 234,567 records, indexed + images)
- FamilySearch digitized volume 005221388: 402 images of 1889-1907 homestead final proofs, 74% name-indexed
- BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov): land patents searchable by name, free
- Originals: NARA Washington D.C., Record Group 49

### Vital records
- No statewide civil registration during territorial period (1890-1907)
- County marriage records from county formation: Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995 (coll. 2134789, 456,789 records, indexed + images)
- Statewide birth/death registration began 1908 (post-statehood)
- Pre-registration alternatives: church records, newspaper notices, territorial court records

### Indian Territory vital and enrollment records
- Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959 (coll. 1987432, 567,890 records, indexed + images)
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets: FamilySearch vol. 005221389, 176 images, BROWSE-ONLY (0% indexed)

### Church records
- Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965 (coll. 1654321, 123,456 records, indexed + images)
- Post-1889 local church registers largely physical at churches or denominational archives

### Census records
- 1890 federal census destroyed; Oklahoma Territory 1890 Special Census at Oklahoma Historical Society
- 1900 and 1910 federal censuses: indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- Dawes Rolls function as census equivalent for Indian Territory residents

### Probate and court records
- Oklahoma Territory district court records at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives
- Include probate, naturalization, civil and criminal cases
- Largely physical only

### Military records
- Service records, pensions: NARA Washington; Fold3 (subscription)
- Spanish-American War (1898) territorial troops

### Cemetery records
- FindAGrave: broad Oklahoma coverage, free
- Physical sexton records at counties, municipalities, local churches

### Newspaper records
- Newspapers.com (subscription); Library of Congress Chronicling America (free, partial)
- Homestead final proof legal notices published in territorial papers

### Immigration and naturalization
- Territorial court naturalizations at NARA Fort Worth (pre-1906)
- Federal district court naturalizations post-1906
- Passenger manifests on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Tax records
- County tax rolls from 1890 onward; substitute for destroyed 1890 federal census
- Physical at county courthouses and Oklahoma State Archives

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 4 indexed collections; 2 digitized volumes | Free |
| BLM GLO Records | Land patents | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1900, 1910; Oklahoma collections | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Oklahoma newspapers 1889+ | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Partial territorial newspaper digitization | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Fort Worth, TX | District court, Dawes Commission, probate, naturalization | In-person / mail |
| NARA Washington D.C. | GLO records, homestead case files | In-person / mail |
| Oklahoma State Archives | Territorial and state records | In-person / mail |
| Oklahoma Historical Society | 1890 territorial census, newspapers, manuscripts | In-person / some digital |
| County courthouses | Deeds, marriages, probate, tax | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial district court case files
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (browse-only, no index)
- County tax rolls 1890-1899
- 1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census (largely physical)
- Early post-1889 church registers
- Rejected homestead application files

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census destroyed 1921; Oklahoma Territory Special Census at OHS is a critical substitute
- Some early county courthouse records lost to fire or flood; verify county-by-county

## Research tips
- Start with the full homestead case file at NARA, not just the BLM patent record
- Determine Oklahoma Territory vs. Indian Territory jurisdiction before searching archives
- Search territorial newspapers for homestead final proof legal notices
- Trace backward to departure states (Kansas, Texas, Missouri) for pre-1889 records
- For possible tribal members, start with FamilySearch collection 1987432 (indexed Dawes Rolls)
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census at OHS is one of the few surviving 1890-era enumerations nationally

## Alabama Region, ~1800 (Pre-Statehood) — Locality Research Guide

The guide has been saved to your project as `loc_001`.

### The short answer on browsable digitized volumes

**FamilySearch has none for this era.** A volume search returned zero results for both "Alabama, United States" and "Mississippi Territory, United States" in the 1780–1820 window. This reflects a real digitization gap, not a tool problem. The four FamilySearch indexed collections that *do* exist (marriages, probate, church records, census substitute indexes) all begin 1803–1810 and are name-indexed, not browsable image volumes.

---

### Jurisdictional Context

The "Alabama region" around 1800 wasn't one place administratively:

| Period | Southern/Coastal Alabama | Interior Alabama |
|---|---|---|
| ~1780–1813 | **Spanish West Florida** (Mobile) | — |
| 1798–1817 | — | **Mississippi Territory** |
| 1813–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** (added) | |
| 1817–1819 | **Alabama Territory** | **Alabama Territory** |

Records follow these jurisdictions, not modern state lines.

---

### Where to Look

**Online/digitized:**
- **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) — land patent records, strong for this period
- **NARA pension files via Fold3** — Revolutionary War and War of 1812 pensions for settlers who served
- **FamilySearch indexed collections** — marriages (1803+), probate (1809+), early church records, census substitute indexes

**Physical archives (not yet digitized):**
- **Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery)** — territorial court minutes, tax lists, early county records
- **Mobile Cathedral Parish (Cathedral Basilica of the Immaculate Conception)** — colonial Catholic registers from Spanish and French eras
- **European repositories** — French (Archives nationales d'outre-mer) and Spanish (Archivo General de Indias in Seville) colonial records for the Mobile area

---

### Strongest Starting Points

1. **BLM GLO records** — free, online, excellent for placing families on the landscape
2. **NARA pensions** — many early Alabama settlers appear here; often contain family information
3. **Alabama Archives** — write or visit for territorial-era records not yet online
4. **Mobile Cathedral registers** — essential for Catholic families in coastal Alabama; some have been microfilmed

The pre-statehood period is genuinely thin online. Most research here will eventually require direct contact with ADAH or working from microfilm.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood Era (circa 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory established 1817 from the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory; became the state of Alabama 14 December 1819.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial government: St. Stephens (Washington County). Mobile was the principal settled town and Spanish administrative center until 1813.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (U.S. federal territory), organized 1798.
- **Population during period:** The federal census of 1810 counted approximately 9,000 free persons in what became Alabama. Settlement was sparse outside Mobile Bay and the Tombigbee River corridor.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur trade, livestock; cotton cultivation beginning in the Tombigbee corridor.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek/Muscogee (interior), Cherokee (northeast), Choctaw (west); Anglo-American settlers from GA, SC, NC, VA, TN; French Creole and Spanish merchant families at Mobile; free and enslaved African Americans.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant at Mobile, Cathedral Parish from French colonial era); Methodist and Baptist circuit riders entering interior settlements ca. 1800.

## Boundary changes
The Alabama region crossed four distinct governing authorities in this period:
- French Mobile District (1702–1763)
- British West Florida — Mobile area (1763–1780)
- Spanish West Florida — Mobile District (1780–1813)
- Mississippi Territory — interior Alabama (1798–1817), organized into Washington County (1800), Baldwin and Madison counties (1809)
- Alabama Territory (1817–1819)

Records follow the governing authority, not modern boundaries. A record from 1805 near the Tombigbee River is filed under Washington County, Mississippi Territory.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- No civil registration existed. Alabama did not begin statewide civil registration until 1908.
- Earliest civil marriage records begin in 1809 at county level (Washington, Baldwin counties).
- FamilySearch collection 1598408 'Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950' covers from 1809 onward (indexed + images).
- Pre-registration alternative: Catholic church registers in Mobile.

### Church records
- Catholic sacramental registers at Mobile Cathedral Parish run from the French colonial era continuously through statehood — baptisms, marriages, burials.
- Methodist and Baptist registers sparse for this period.
- FamilySearch collection 1986396 'Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950' (78,394 images); earliest records from 1803.
- French colonial registers: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- Spanish-era registers (1780–1813): Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress.
- Language: French (colonial), Spanish/Latin (Spanish era), English (Anglo-American Protestant).

### Census records
- 1810 federal census: earliest to enumerate any Alabama settlement (Washington County, MS Territory).
- Mississippi Territory censuses 1801, 1805, 1808: held at ADAH; not confirmed in any digitized online database.
- Spanish padrones (Mobile District): Archivo General de Indias; copies at Library of Congress.
- FamilySearch collection 2016756 'Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890' (index only, no images, begins 1810).

### Probate and court records
